<style>
.gl-controls {
  display: flex;
  flex-direction: column;
  gap: 0.9rem;
  margin-bottom: 1.5rem;
  padding-bottom: 1.25rem;
  border-bottom: 1px solid #e8e0d4;
}

.sort-btn { font-size: 0.78rem; padding: 0.22rem 0.6rem; border: 1px solid #c8bfaf; border-radius: 3px; background: transparent; color: #888; cursor: pointer; display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 0.25rem; }

.imp-btn.active.imp-core-btn  { background: #5a3a2a; color: #faf8f5; border-color: #5a3a2a; }

.imp-btn.active.imp-expert-btn { background: #3a4a62; color: #faf8f5; border-color: #3a4a62; }
.term-entry { border-top: 1px solid #e8e0d4; padding: 1.1rem 0; cursor: pointer; }
.term-entry:last-of-type { border-bottom: 1px solid #e8e0d4; }

.term-pronunciation { font-size: 0.8rem; color: #999; font-style: italic; }
.term-cats { display: flex; gap: 0.3rem; flex-wrap: wrap; margin-left: auto; }
.term-cat { font-size: 0.68rem; padding: 0.12rem 0.45rem; background: #f0ebe2; border-radius: 2rem; color: #5a4a30; text-transform: uppercase; letter-spacing: 0.04em; }

.condensed-table.active { display: table; }
.condensed-table th { text-align: left; font-size: 0.72rem; text-transform: uppercase; letter-spacing: 0.07em; color: #aaa; padding: 0.4rem 0.5rem; border-bottom: 1px solid #e8e0d4; font-weight: 400; }
.condensed-table td { padding: 0.55rem 0.5rem; border-bottom: 1px solid #f0ebe2; vertical-align: top; color: #2c2416; }
.condensed-table tr { cursor: pointer; }
.condensed-table tr:hover td { background: #faf6f0; }
.ct-term { font-weight: 600; font-family: 'Playfair Display', Georgia, serif; white-space: nowrap; padding-right: 1rem; }
.ct-def { color: #555; }
.condensed-expanded { display: none; background: #faf6f0; }
.condensed-expanded.open { display: table-row; }
.condensed-expanded td { padding: 0.75rem 0.5rem; border-bottom: 1px solid #e8e0d4; font-size: 0.86rem; }

.imp-badge { display: none !important; }
.gl-row:has(.imp-filter) { display: none !important; }
.sort-btn[data-key="importance"] { display: none !important; }
</style>

<!-- ── Roman Numerals ── -->

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="roman-numeral" data-importance="core">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="vii">VII</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[sɛvən]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Roman Numerals</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-core">Core</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">The seventh scale degree or a chord built on it.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>In Roman numeral analysis, VII (or vii°) denotes the seventh degree of
the scale and the chord built on it. In major keys, the seventh degree
is a leading tone a half step below the tonic; the triad built on it is
diminished. Uppercase numerals indicate major quality; lowercase indicate
minor.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_numeral_analysis" target="_blank">1</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="roman-numeral" data-importance="core">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="vi">VI</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[sɪks]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Roman Numerals</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-core">Core</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">The sixth scale degree or a chord built on it.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>VI denotes the sixth scale degree (the submediant) and the chord built
on it. In major keys, this chord is minor (vi); when written in uppercase
(VI), it refers to a major chord on the sixth degree, common in minor
keys and as a chromatic alteration.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_numeral_analysis" target="_blank">1</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="roman-numeral" data-importance="core">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="iv">IV</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[fɔːɹ]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Roman Numerals</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-core">Core</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">The subdominant — the fourth scale degree or a chord built on it.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>IV denotes the subdominant — the fourth degree of the scale. The
subdominant chord moves naturally toward either the dominant (V) or
directly to the tonic (I), the latter producing a plagal cadence.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_numeral_analysis" target="_blank">1</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="roman-numeral" data-importance="core">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="v">V</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[faɪv]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Roman Numerals</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-core">Core</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">The dominant — the fifth scale degree or a chord built on it.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>V denotes the dominant — the fifth degree of the scale and the most
harmonically active chord in tonal music. The dominant triad (V) or
seventh chord (V7) creates strong tension that resolves to the tonic (I).
The V–I progression is the foundation of tonal cadential motion.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_numeral_analysis" target="_blank">1</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="roman-numeral" data-importance="core">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="iii">III</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[θɹiː]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Roman Numerals</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-core">Core</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">The mediant — the third scale degree or a chord built on it.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>III denotes the mediant — the third degree of the scale, midway between
the tonic and dominant. In major keys the mediant chord is minor (iii);
uppercase III refers to a major chord on the third degree, typical in
minor keys.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_numeral_analysis" target="_blank">1</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="roman-numeral" data-importance="core">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="ii">II</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[tuː]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Roman Numerals</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-core">Core</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">The supertonic — the second scale degree or a chord built on it.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>II denotes the supertonic — the second degree of the scale. In major
keys, the supertonic chord is minor (ii) and functions as a
pre-dominant, often preceding V. The II chord (uppercase, major) appears
frequently as a secondary dominant or in modal contexts.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_numeral_analysis" target="_blank">1</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="roman-numeral" data-importance="core">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="i">I</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[wʌn]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Roman Numerals</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-core">Core</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">The tonic — the home chord, built on the first scale degree.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>I denotes the tonic — the first scale degree and the chord built on it.
The tonic chord is the harmonic center of gravity in tonal music; most
pieces begin and end on I. In major keys it is a major triad; in minor
keys it is minor (i).</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_numeral_analysis" target="_blank">1</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="italian" data-importance="core">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="a-cappella">a cappella</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[ɑː kəpˈɛlə]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Italian</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-core">Core</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">Vocal music performed without instrumental accompaniment.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>Italian: "in the manner of the chapel." Choral or ensemble singing
performed entirely without instrumental accompaniment. The term is also
applied to solo vocal music without accompaniment. Common in Renaissance
sacred music, barbershop, and contemporary a cappella groups.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_cappella" target="_blank">1</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="italian" data-importance="core">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="accelerando">accelerando</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[ætʃˌɛləɹˈɑːndoʊ]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Italian</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-core">Core</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">Gradually getting faster.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>Italian: "accelerating." A tempo direction indicating that the music
should gradually increase in speed. Abbreviated accel. The opposite
is ritardando (or rallentando): gradually slowing down.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Accelerando" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#tempo">tempo</a>, <a href="#rubato">rubato</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="italian" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="acciaccatura">acciaccatura</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[ətʃˌɑːkətʃˈʊəɹə]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Italian</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">A very short ornamental note played just before the main note.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>Italian: "crushing." A grace note written as a small note with a stroke
through its stem, played as briefly as possible immediately before the
main note — so quickly that it has almost no duration of its own.
Distinguished from the appoggiatura, which is held for a portion of the
main note's value and falls on the beat.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acciaccatura" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#appoggiatura">appoggiatura</a>, <a href="#ornamentation">ornamentation</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="acoustic-instrument">acoustic instrument</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[əkˈuːstɪk ˈɪnstɹʊmənt]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">An instrument that produces sound by acoustic (non-electronic) means.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>An instrument that generates sound entirely through acoustic physical
processes — vibrating strings, air columns, membranes, or the body of
the instrument itself — without electronic amplification or signal
processing. Contrasted with electric instruments (which require
amplification) and electronic instruments (which generate sound
electronically).</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acoustic_music" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#aerophone">aerophone</a>, <a href="#chordophone">chordophone</a>, <a href="#idiophone">idiophone</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="italian" data-importance="core">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="adagio">adagio</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[ədˈɑːdʒioʊ]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Italian</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-core">Core</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">Slow and stately; a slow tempo marking.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>Italian: "at ease." A tempo marking indicating a slow, stately pace —
slower than andante but faster than largo. Also used as a noun to
describe a slow movement (e.g., "the adagio of the symphony").</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tempo" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#tempo">tempo</a>, <a href="#allegro">allegro</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="technology" data-importance="expert">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="adsr">ADSR</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[eɪ diː ɛs ɑːɹ]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Technology</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-expert">Expert</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">The four stages of a synthesizer envelope: Attack, Decay, Sustain, Release.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>The four parameters describing the shape of a synthesizer envelope —
the control signal that shapes how a sound changes over time. Attack
is the time to reach peak level; decay is the time to fall to the
sustain level; sustain is the held level while a key is pressed; release
is the time to fall to silence after the key is released. ADSR envelopes
typically control amplitude, filter cutoff, and pitch.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envelope_(music)" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#envelope-curve">envelope curve</a>, <a href="#synthesis">synthesis</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="aerophone">aerophone</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[ˈɛɹəfoʊn]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">An instrument that produces sound through a vibrating column of air.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>One of the four primary instrument categories in the Hornbostel-Sachs
classification. Aerophones produce sound through the vibration of an
air column. Includes free aerophones (harmonica, accordion), where the
air vibrates without a tube, and tube aerophones (flute, trumpet,
oboe), where the air column is enclosed.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aerophone" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#chordophone">chordophone</a>, <a href="#idiophone">idiophone</a>, <a href="#membranophone">membranophone</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="non-western" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="alap">alap</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[ˈɑːlɑːp]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Non-Western</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">The slow, unmetered introductory section of a raga performance.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>The opening section of a North Indian classical music performance, in
which the performer introduces and explores the notes and character of
the raga in free rhythm, without percussion accompaniment. The alap
establishes the raga's mood (rasa) before the metered sections begin.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alap" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#raga">raga</a>, <a href="#bandish">bandish</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="aleatoric-aleatory-music">aleatoric/aleatory music</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[ˌeɪliˈætɒɹɪk]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">Music incorporating elements of chance or unpredictability in its composition or performance.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>Music in which elements of chance or indeterminacy play a role — either
in the compositional process or in performance. Key figures include
John Cage (<strong>Music of Changes</strong>, 1951, composed using the I Ching) and
Witold Lutosławski (controlled aleatorism, where individual players
improvise within defined limits while the ensemble is coordinated).
Distinct from pure improvisation by the presence of some structural
framework.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aleatoric_music" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#improvising">improvising</a>, <a href="#chance-music">chance music</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="italian" data-importance="core">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="allegretto">allegretto</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[ˌæləɡɹˈɛtoʊ]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Italian</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-core">Core</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">Moderately fast; slightly slower than allegro.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>Italian: diminutive of allegro. A tempo marking indicating a moderately
brisk pace — lighter and slightly slower than allegro, but faster than
andante. Often implies a lighter character than allegro.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tempo" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#allegro">allegro</a>, <a href="#tempo">tempo</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="italian" data-importance="core">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="allegro">allegro</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[əlˈɛɡɹoʊ]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Italian</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-core">Core</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">Fast and lively; one of the most common tempo markings.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>Italian: "merry, lively." A tempo marking indicating a fast, lively
pace. One of the most common movement designations in Western classical
music. Qualified forms include allegro ma non troppo (fast but not too
much), allegro vivace (fast and vivacious), and allegro moderato.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tempo" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#adagio">adagio</a>, <a href="#tempo">tempo</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="antiphonal">antiphonal</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[ænˈtɪfənəl]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">Involving alternation between two groups of performers.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>A performance practice in which two groups of performers alternate,
answer, or respond to each other. Common in Gregorian chant (antiphonal
chanting), Renaissance polychoral music (e.g., the double-choir works
of Giovanni Gabrieli at St. Mark's Venice), and gospel call-and-response
performance.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antiphony" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#call-and-response">call and response</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="italian" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="appoggiatura">appoggiatura</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[əˌpɒdʒətʃˈʊəɹə]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Italian</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">An ornamental note on the beat that displaces the main note and resolves by step.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>Italian: "leaning." A grace note that falls on the beat, displacing the
main note and taking a portion of its value before resolving by step
(usually downward). The appoggiatura creates a temporary dissonance that
adds expressive intensity. Distinguished from the acciaccatura by its
rhythmic weight — it is heard clearly rather than crushed through.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appoggiatura" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#acciaccatura">acciaccatura</a>, <a href="#suspensions">suspensions</a>, <a href="#ornamentation">ornamentation</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="italian" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="arco">arco</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[ˈɑːɹkoʊ]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Italian</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">A direction to resume playing with the bow (after pizzicato).</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>Italian: "bow." A performance direction for string players indicating
that the bow should be used, typically appearing after a passage of
pizzicato (plucked) playing.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arco" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#pizzicato">pizzicato</a>, <a href="#con-arco">con arco</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="italian" data-importance="core">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="aria">aria</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[ˈɑːɹiə]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Italian</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-core">Core</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">A self-contained song for solo voice in an opera, oratorio, or cantata.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>Italian: "air." A formal, self-contained composition for solo voice,
typically with orchestral accompaniment, in an opera, oratorio, or
cantata. Arias are usually more melodically elaborate than recitative
and allow the soloist to express a character's emotional state at length.
Common forms include the Baroque da capo aria (A–B–A structure).</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aria" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#recitative">recitative</a>, <a href="#cantata">cantata</a>, <a href="#opera">opera</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="italian" data-importance="core">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="arpeggio">arpeggio</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[ɑːɹpˈɛdʒioʊ]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Italian</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-core">Core</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">The notes of a chord played in succession rather than simultaneously.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>Italian: "in the manner of a harp." The notes of a chord played one
after another rather than all at once, either ascending or descending.
Arpeggios are used in both melody and accompaniment and are foundational
to techniques such as Alberti bass. Distinct from broken chord only in
the consistent direction of movement.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arpeggio" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#broken-chord">broken chord</a>, <a href="#chord">chord</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="atonal">atonal</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[eɪˈtoʊnəl]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">Music that avoids establishing a tonal center.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>Music that avoids organizing pitch around a central tonic, rejecting
the hierarchy of tonal harmony. Developed most systematically by
Schoenberg and the Second Viennese School in the early 20th century.
Free atonality (1908–1923) preceded the more systematic twelve-tone
technique. Atonal music uses all twelve chromatic pitches without
implying a home key.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atonality" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#12-note-techniques">12-note techniques</a>, <a href="#tonality">tonality</a>, <a href="#non-tonal">non-tonal</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="harmony" data-importance="core">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="augmentation">augmentation</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[ˌɔːɡmɛnˈteɪʃən]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Harmony</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-core">Core</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">Restating a theme with all note values lengthened.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>A contrapuntal and developmental technique in which a melody or motif
is restated with all rhythmic values increased — typically doubled.
The opposite is diminution (values shortened). Augmentation is common
in fugue and in development sections.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augmentation_(music)" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#diminution">diminution</a>, <a href="#fugue">fugue</a>, <a href="#development">development</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="augmented">augmented</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[ɔːɡˈmɛntɪd]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">An interval or chord enlarged by a half step beyond its major or perfect form.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>An interval quality one semitone larger than a major or perfect interval
of the same number. An augmented fourth (tritone) is a half step larger
than a perfect fourth; an augmented sixth chord is a chromatic harmony
built on the flattened sixth degree. Augmented triads contain a major
third and an augmented fifth.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augmented_interval" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#interval">interval</a>, <a href="#diminished">diminished</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="authentic-perfect-cadence">authentic (perfect) cadence</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[ɔːˈθɛntɪk kˈeɪdəns]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">A cadence moving from V to I — the strongest harmonic close in tonal music.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>The strongest cadential formula in tonal music: the dominant chord (V
or V7) resolving to the tonic (I). A perfect authentic cadence (PAC)
requires both chords in root position and the tonic note in the highest
voice at the point of resolution; an imperfect authentic cadence (IAC)
does not meet all these conditions. The V–I resolution is the
fundamental engine of tonal music.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cadence_(music)" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#cadence">cadence</a>, <a href="#plagal-cadence">plagal cadence</a>, <a href="#v">V</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="balophone">balophone</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[bˈæləfoʊn]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">A West African xylophone-like instrument with gourd resonators beneath wooden bars.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>A West African idiophone consisting of wooden bars of varying lengths
struck with mallets, with hollow gourd resonators suspended beneath each
bar. The balafon (also spelled balophone) is traditional in Mande, Gur,
and other West African musical cultures. A cousin of the marimba and
xylophone, it produces a warm, resonant tone.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balafon" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#idiophone">idiophone</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="non-western" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="balungan">balungan</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[bɑːˈlʊŋɑːn]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Non-Western</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">The core melodic framework of a Javanese gamelan composition.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>In Javanese gamelan music, the balungan is the skeletal melody that
forms the structural basis of a composition. Other instruments in the
ensemble elaborate, ornament, and subdivide the balungan according to
their role in the texture. The balungan is typically played by
metallophone instruments such as the saron and slenthem.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balungan" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#gamelan">gamelan</a>, <a href="#slendro">slendro</a>, <a href="#pelog">pelog</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="non-western" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="bandish">bandish</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[ˈbɑːndɪʃ]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Non-Western</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">A fixed, composed piece within Hindustani classical music, providing the rhythmic and melodic framework for improvisation.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>In North Indian (Hindustani) classical music, a bandish (also called
gat) is a composed, fixed piece that establishes the rhythmic cycle
(tala) and provides material for improvisation. After the free-rhythm
alap, the bandish introduces the tabla and marks the transition to
metered playing.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bandish" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#alap">alap</a>, <a href="#raga">raga</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="non-western" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="bansuri">bansuri</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[ˈbɑːnsʊɹiː]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Non-Western</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">A transverse bamboo flute used in North Indian classical music.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>A side-blown bamboo flute central to Hindustani classical music and
associated with the deity Krishna. It has no keys — pitch and microtonal
inflection are controlled entirely through embouchure and finger
technique. The virtuoso Hariprasad Chaurasia is among the instrument's
most celebrated modern exponents.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bansuri" target="_blank">1</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="homograph" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="bass-instrument-register">bass (instrument/register)</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[beɪs]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Homograph</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">The lowest register of pitch; also a family of low-pitched instruments.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>In music, "bass" (rhymes with "face") refers to the low register of
sound, the lowest voice in a harmonic texture, or instruments and voices
that occupy that range. Distinct from the fish (rhymes with "mass").
The bass voice is the lowest male singing voice; bass instruments include
double bass, bass guitar, bassoon, tuba, and bass clarinet.</p>
    <p>Note: This entry overrides the fish pronunciation globally. Use the
inline bracket syntax [[text][/ipa/]] for fish references in source files.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bass_(music)" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#basso-continuo">basso continuo</a>, <a href="#bass-clef">bass clef</a>, <a href="#walking-bass">walking bass</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="italian" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="basso-continuo">basso continuo</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[ˈbæsoʊ kənˈtɪnjuoʊ]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Italian</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">The harmonic bass-line foundation of Baroque music, typically played by keyboard and bass instrument together.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>Italian: "continuous bass." A Baroque performance practice in which a
bass line (played by cello, bass viol, or bassoon) is combined with a
keyboard instrument (harpsichord, organ, lute) that improvises harmony
above the written bass, guided by figured bass notation. The continuo
group provides the harmonic and rhythmic foundation for nearly all
Baroque ensemble music.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basso_continuo" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#figured-bass">figured bass</a>, <a href="#ground-bass">ground bass</a>, <a href="#walking-bass">walking bass</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="beat">beat</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[biːt]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">The basic unit of musical time that listeners tap along to.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>The basic recurring pulse of music — what listeners tap their feet to.
Beats are organized into metres (groups of strong and weak beats).
The tempo indicates how fast the beat moves (beats per minute, BPM).
In most popular music, beats 2 and 4 in 4/4 metre are accented (the
backbeat).</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_(music)" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#metre">metre</a>, <a href="#tempo">tempo</a>, <a href="#pulse">pulse</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="binary-form">binary form</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[bˈaɪnəɹi fɔːɹm]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">A two-part musical structure: A–B.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>A musical form consisting of two sections (A and B), usually both
repeated. Simple binary form has two contrasting sections; rounded
binary has a return of the opening material near the end of the B
section (anticipating ternary and sonata form). Characteristic of
Baroque dance movements (sarabande, allemande, etc.).</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binary_form" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#ternary-form">ternary form</a>, <a href="#sonata-form">sonata form</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="blue-notes">blue notes</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[bluː noʊts]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">Flattened or bent pitches (particularly the 3rd, 5th, and 7th) characteristic of the blues.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>Notes that are flattened or bent slightly below the standard pitch of
a major scale, particularly the third, fifth, and seventh scale degrees.
Central to the blues and derived styles (jazz, R&B, rock). On instruments
capable of continuous pitch variation (guitar, voice, harmonica), blue
notes are bent rather than played at a fixed pitch, giving them
expressive ambiguity between major and minor.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_note" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#blues-scale">blues scale</a>, <a href="#bent-notes">bent notes</a>, <a href="#microtone">microtone</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="broken-chord">broken chord</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[bɹˈoʊkən kɔːɹd]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">The notes of a chord played one at a time rather than simultaneously.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>A chord whose notes are played in sequence rather than simultaneously.
Used interchangeably with arpeggio, though some distinguish between the
two: an arpeggio moves consistently upward or downward, while a broken
chord may move in a freer or repeating pattern (e.g., Alberti bass).</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arpeggio" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#arpeggio">arpeggio</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="harmony" data-importance="core">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="cadence">cadence</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[kˈeɪdəns]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Harmony</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-core">Core</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">A harmonic progression that creates a sense of arrival, pause, or conclusion.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>A sequence of two or more chords that creates a sense of arrival,
punctuation, or conclusion. The four main cadence types in tonal music
are: authentic/perfect (V–I, strongest close), plagal (IV–I, "Amen"),
half/imperfect (ending on V), and deceptive/interrupted (V resolving to
vi or another unexpected chord).</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cadence_(music)" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#authentic-perfect-cadence">authentic cadence</a>, <a href="#plagal-cadence">plagal cadence</a>, <a href="#half-imperfect-cadence">half cadence</a>, <a href="#deceptive-interrupted-cadence">deceptive cadence</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="cadenza">cadenza</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[kəˈdɛnzə]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">An unaccompanied virtuosic passage for the soloist, typically near the end of a concerto movement.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>Italian: "cadence." A virtuosic solo passage, usually unaccompanied,
occurring near the end of a movement in a concerto. The orchestra
pauses on a sustained chord (typically a 6/4 chord on the dominant)
while the soloist improvises or performs a written-out cadenza before
resolving to the final cadence. Historical cadenzas were improvised;
later composers wrote them out.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cadenza" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#concerto">concerto</a>, <a href="#cadence">cadence</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="core">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="canon">canon</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[kˈænən]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-core">Core</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">A contrapuntal form in which the same melody is imitated by subsequent voices at a fixed time interval.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>A contrapuntal technique in which a melody in one voice is exactly
imitated by one or more following voices entering at a fixed time
interval (and sometimes at a different pitch). The strictest form of
imitation. Pachelbel's Canon in D, "Frère Jacques", and "Row Your Boat"
are familiar examples. A round is a canon in which the imitation is
at the unison or octave.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canon_(music)" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#imitation">imitation</a>, <a href="#fugue">fugue</a>, <a href="#counterpoint">counterpoint</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="italian" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="cantabile">cantabile</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[kænˈtɑːbɪleɪ]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Italian</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">In a singing, lyrical style.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>Italian: "singable, in a singing style." A direction to perform in a
smooth, lyrical, song-like manner, with expressive phrasing. Often
applied to instrumental music to indicate that the player should imitate
the quality and flow of a singing voice.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cantabile" target="_blank">1</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="italian" data-importance="core">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="cantata">cantata</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[kænˈtɑːtə]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Italian</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-core">Core</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">A multi-movement vocal work for voices and instruments.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>Italian: "sung piece." A vocal composition of several movements for
soloists, chorus, and instruments, typically setting a sacred or secular
text. Bach's church cantatas are the most celebrated examples of the
genre. Distinguished from the oratorio primarily by its shorter length
and (often) liturgical function.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cantata" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#aria">aria</a>, <a href="#recitative">recitative</a>, <a href="#chorale">chorale</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="harmony" data-importance="core">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="chorale">chorale</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[kɒˈɹɑːl]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Harmony</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-core">Core</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">A hymn tune, especially one harmonized in four voices; also a choir.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>(1) A hymn tune of the German Lutheran tradition, typically in four-part
(SATB) harmony. Bach's chorale harmonizations are among the most
studied examples of tonal voice leading. (2) In some usages, a choral
ensemble or the choral section of a larger work.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chorale" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#cantata">cantata</a>, <a href="#harmony">harmony</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="chordophone">chordophone</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[kˈɔːɹdəfoʊn]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">An instrument that produces sound through vibrating strings.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>One of the four primary instrument categories in the Hornbostel-Sachs
classification system. Chordophones produce sound through the vibration
of one or more stretched strings. Subdivided into simple chordophones
(musical bows, zithers) and composite chordophones (lutes, harps,
lyres). Includes guitar, violin, piano, harp, and sitar.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chordophone" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#idiophone">idiophone</a>, <a href="#membranophone">membranophone</a>, <a href="#aerophone">aerophone</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="core">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="chromatic">chromatic</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[kɹoʊˈmætɪk]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-core">Core</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">Using notes or intervals outside the prevailing diatonic scale.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>Relating to pitches, intervals, or harmonies that include notes outside
a given diatonic scale. The chromatic scale divides the octave into
twelve equal semitones. Chromatic notes add color and tension;
chromaticism is characteristic of late Romantic music (Wagner, Liszt)
and jazz harmony.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromatic_scale" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#diatonic">diatonic</a>, <a href="#enharmonic">enharmonic</a>, <a href="#modulation-in-music">modulation</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="italian" data-importance="core">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="coda">coda</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[ˈkoʊdə]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Italian</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-core">Core</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">A concluding section added to the end of a formal structure.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>Italian: "tail." A passage that brings a movement or section to a
conclusion, following the main formal structure. In sonata form, the
coda follows the recapitulation and may be brief or substantially
extended (as in Beethoven). The coda symbol (𝄌) is used in lead sheets
and popular music to indicate a jump to a concluding section.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coda_(music)" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#sonata-form">sonata form</a>, <a href="#recapitulation">recapitulation</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="compound-metre">compound metre</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[kˈɒmpaʊnd mˈiːtəɹ]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">A metre in which each beat divides into three equal parts (e.g. 6/8, 9/8, 12/8).</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>A metric organization in which each beat naturally divides into three
equal subunits (as opposed to simple metre, where beats divide into
two). Time signatures 6/8, 9/8, and 12/8 are compound duple, triple,
and quadruple metre respectively. The characteristic lilt of 6/8 is
foundational to jigs, barcarolles, and many folk traditions.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metre_(music)" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#metre">metre</a>, <a href="#time-signature">time signature</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="italian" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="con-arco">con arco</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[kɒn ˈɑːɹkoʊ]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Italian</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">With the bow (resume bowed playing).</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>Italian: "with the bow." A direction for string players to resume playing
with the bow after a pizzicato passage. Equivalent to arco.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arco" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#arco">arco</a>, <a href="#pizzicato">pizzicato</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="italian" data-importance="core">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="concerto">concerto</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[kənˈtʃɛɹtoʊ]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Italian</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-core">Core</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">A multi-movement work for soloist and orchestra.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>A large-scale composition featuring one or more soloists in contrast
with an orchestra. The standard Classical concerto has three movements
(fast–slow–fast) and typically includes a cadenza — an unaccompanied
solo passage — near the end of the first movement. The solo-orchestra
dialogue is central to the form.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concerto" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#concerto-grosso">concerto grosso</a>, <a href="#cadenza">cadenza</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="italian" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="concerto-grosso">concerto grosso</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[kənˈtʃɛɹtoʊ ˈɡɹɒsoʊ]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Italian</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">A Baroque form contrasting a small group of soloists with a larger orchestra.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>Italian: "large concerto." A Baroque form in which a small group of
soloists (the concertino) is contrasted with the full ensemble (the
ripieno or tutti). Handel's Op. 6 and Corelli's Op. 6 concerti grossi
are central examples of the genre.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concerto_grosso" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#concerto">concerto</a>, <a href="#basso-continuo">basso continuo</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="core">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="consonance">consonance</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[kˈɒnsənəns]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-core">Core</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">An interval or chord that sounds stable and resolved.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>Intervals and chords perceived as stable, restful, and resolved in
tonal music. Perfect consonances include the unison, octave, perfect
fifth, and perfect fourth; imperfect consonances include thirds and
sixths. What is considered consonant has varied across historical periods
and musical cultures.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consonance_and_dissonance" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#dissonance">dissonance</a>, <a href="#interval">interval</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="italian" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="con-sordino">con sordino</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[kɒn sɔːɹˈdiːnoʊ]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Italian</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">With mute.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>Italian: "with mute." A direction to apply a mute to an instrument,
dampening and altering the timbre. On strings, a mute clamps onto the
bridge; on brass, a mute is inserted into the bell. The opposite is
senza sordino ("without mute").</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mute_(music)" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#mute">mute</a>, <a href="#timbre">timbre</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="core">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="counterpoint">counterpoint</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[kˈaʊntəɹpɔɪnt]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-core">Core</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">The technique of combining two or more independent melodic voices simultaneously.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>The art of combining two or more independent melodic lines so that they
sound simultaneously while following rules of consonance, dissonance,
and voice leading. Species counterpoint (Fux's system) codifies the
rules from Renaissance practice. Counterpoint is the foundation of
fugue, canon, and much of Western classical composition.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counterpoint" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#polyphony">polyphony</a>, <a href="#fugue">fugue</a>, <a href="#imitation">imitation</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="italian" data-importance="core">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="crescendo">crescendo</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[kɹəˈʃɛndoʊ]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Italian</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-core">Core</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">Gradually getting louder.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>Italian: "growing." A dynamic direction to gradually increase in volume.
Notated by the "hairpin" symbol (<). Often used informally (and
inaccurately) to refer simply to a loud climax; strictly, it refers to
the process of getting louder, not the arrival.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynamics_(music)" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#decrescendo">decrescendo</a>, <a href="#dynamics">dynamics</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="cross-rhythms">cross rhythms</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[kɹɒs ˈɹɪðəmz]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">Conflicting rhythmic patterns that create tension against the prevailing metre.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>The simultaneous use of contrasting rhythmic patterns that conflict
with the prevailing metre or with each other. Often used interchangeably
with polyrhythm, though cross-rhythm may refer specifically to a pattern
that contradicts the notated metre rather than two equal-status competing
metres. Central to African drumming, Latin music, and jazz.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross-rhythm" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#polyrhythm">polyrhythm</a>, <a href="#hemiola">hemiola</a>, <a href="#syncopation">syncopation</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="technology" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="daw">DAW</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[dɔː]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Technology</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">Digital audio workstation — software for recording, editing, and producing audio.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>An application for recording, editing, arranging, mixing, and mastering
audio. DAWs replace the traditional recording studio's tape machines,
mixing desks, and outboard gear with software equivalents. Common DAWs
include Pro Tools, Logic Pro, Ableton Live, GarageBand, FL Studio, and
Reaper.</p>
    <p>Note on pronunciation: "daw" (single syllable) is common; "D-A-W"
(spelled out) is also used. Change the IPA to /diː eɪ dʌbᵊljuː/ if you
prefer the spelled-out version.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_audio_workstation" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#recording">recording</a>, <a href="#mixing">mixing</a>, <a href="#sequencer">sequencer</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="italian" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="decrescendo">decrescendo</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[ˌdiːkɹəˈʃɛndoʊ]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Italian</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">Gradually getting softer.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>A dynamic direction to gradually decrease in volume. Synonymous with
diminuendo. Notated by the reverse hairpin symbol (>).</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynamics_(music)" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#crescendo">crescendo</a>, <a href="#dynamics">dynamics</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="development">development</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[dɪˈvɛləpmənt]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">(1) The middle section of sonata form; (2) the manipulation and transformation of musical material.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>(1) In sonata form: the middle section following the exposition, in
which the themes are fragmented, combined, transposed, and transformed
through a variety of keys, creating tension before the recapitulation.
(2) More broadly, any compositional process of elaborating and
transforming musical material — through sequence, fragmentation,
augmentation, diminution, etc.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Development_(music)" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#sonata-form">sonata form</a>, <a href="#exposition">exposition</a>, <a href="#recapitulation">recapitulation</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="harmony" data-importance="core">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="diatonic">diatonic</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[ˌdaɪəˈtɒnɪk]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Harmony</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-core">Core</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">Belonging to, or derived from, the notes of a major or minor scale.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>Relating to notes, intervals, chords, or harmonies that belong to a
given major or minor scale without chromatic alteration. Diatonic harmony
uses only the chords naturally occurring in a key (I through VII).
Contrasted with chromatic, which introduces notes from outside the scale.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diatonic_scale" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#chromatic">chromatic</a>, <a href="#tonality">tonality</a>, <a href="#scale-degrees">scale degrees</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="diatonic-harmony">diatonic harmony</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[ˌdaɪəˈtɒnɪk hˈɑːɹməni]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">Harmony using only the chords naturally occurring within a given key.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>Harmony based entirely on the chords naturally formed by the notes of
a major or minor scale, without chromatic alteration. The seven diatonic
triads of a major key are I, ii, iii, IV, V, vi, and vii°. Diatonic
harmony is the foundation of tonal music; chromatic harmony introduces
notes or chords from outside the key.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diatonic_function" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#diatonic">diatonic</a>, <a href="#chromatic">chromatic</a>, <a href="#tonality">tonality</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="core">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="diminuendo">diminuendo</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[dɪˌmɪnjuˈɛndoʊ]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-core">Core</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">Gradually getting softer; synonymous with decrescendo.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>Italian: "diminishing." A dynamic direction to gradually decrease in
volume. Synonymous with decrescendo. Abbreviated dim.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynamics_(music)" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#crescendo">crescendo</a>, <a href="#dynamics">dynamics</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="harmony" data-importance="core">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="diminution">diminution</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[ˌdɪmɪˈnjuːʃən]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Harmony</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-core">Core</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">Restating a theme with all note values shortened.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>A contrapuntal technique in which a melody or motif is restated with
all rhythmic values decreased — typically halved. Creates a sense of
intensification or forward drive. The opposite of augmentation.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diminution" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#augmentation">augmentation</a>, <a href="#fugue">fugue</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="core">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="dissonance">dissonance</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[dˈɪsənəns]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-core">Core</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">An interval or chord that creates tension and feels unstable, requiring resolution.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>In tonal music, intervals and chords perceived as tense or unstable,
creating a need for resolution to consonance. What counts as dissonant
has varied across history and cultures — the perfect fourth was
considered dissonant in medieval counterpoint but is consonant in most
modern contexts. Dissonance and its resolution are the primary drivers
of tension and release in tonal music.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consonance_and_dissonance" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#consonance">consonance</a>, <a href="#suspensions">suspensions</a>, <a href="#resolution">resolution</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="italian" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="dolce">dolce</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[ˈdɒltʃeɪ]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Italian</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">Sweetly; softly and gently.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>Italian: "sweet." A performance direction indicating a gentle, soft,
lyrical character. Often associated with a smooth, expressive tone
quality rather than merely quiet dynamics.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Italian_musical_terms_used_in_English" target="_blank">1</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="core">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="dominant">dominant</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[dˈɒmɪnənt]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-core">Core</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">The fifth scale degree; the chord built on it is the most harmonically active in tonal music.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>The fifth scale degree and the chord built on it. The dominant chord
(V) has a strong tendency to resolve to the tonic (I), making V–I the
most fundamental progression in tonal music. The dominant seventh (V7)
adds a minor seventh above the root, intensifying the pull toward
resolution. The term also refers to the fifth scale degree itself.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominant_(music)" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#v">V</a>, <a href="#scale-degrees">scale degrees</a>, <a href="#authentic-perfect-cadence">authentic cadence</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="drone">drone</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[dɹoʊn]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">A sustained pitch held continuously beneath changing melody or harmony.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>A sustained, continuous pitch (or pitches) held throughout a section or
entire piece, while melody and harmony move above it. Central to Indian
classical music (the tamboura provides the drone), Scottish bagpipes,
and much world music. Also used in experimental and ambient electronic
music. Related to pedal point but typically longer in duration and more
structural.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drone_(music)" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#pedal-tone">pedal tone</a>, <a href="#ostinato">ostinato</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="core">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="dynamics">dynamics</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[daɪˈnæmɪks]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-core">Core</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">The variation in loudness in music, and the markings that indicate these variations.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>The element of music concerned with variations in loudness. Dynamic
markings in Western notation range from ppp (pianissississimo, very
very soft) through pp, p, mp, mf, f, ff to fff (fortississimo). Gradual
changes are marked crescendo (getting louder) and decrescendo/diminuendo
(getting softer). Sudden changes include sforzando (sf/sfz) and
fortepiano (fp).</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynamics_(music)" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#crescendo">crescendo</a>, <a href="#decrescendo">decrescendo</a>, <a href="#sforzando">sforzando</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="harmony" data-importance="core">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="enharmonic">enharmonic</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[ˌɛnhɑːɹˈmɒnɪk]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Harmony</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-core">Core</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">Pitches that sound the same but are spelled differently (e.g. F# and Gb).</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>Notes that are acoustically identical (in equal temperament) but written
differently, such as F# and Gb, or C# and Db. Enharmonic equivalence
is relevant in modulation, chromaticism, and understanding how
instruments like the piano, which has no distinction between F# and Gb,
relate to those that do (fretless strings, voice).</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enharmonic" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#temperament">temperament</a>, <a href="#modulation-in-music">modulation</a>, <a href="#chromatic">chromatic</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="envelope-curve">envelope curve</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[ˈɛnvələʊp kɜːɹv]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">The shape of a sound&#x27;s amplitude over time, described in four stages: Attack, Decay, Sustain, Release.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>The time-varying shape of a sound's amplitude (or other parameter),
typically described by four stages: Attack (rise to peak), Decay (fall
to sustain level), Sustain (held level), and Release (fall to silence).
The ADSR envelope is the most common form and is a primary tool for
shaping synthesized sounds.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envelope_(music)" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#adsr">ADSR</a>, <a href="#synthesis">synthesis</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="eq">EQ</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[iː kjuː]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">Equalization — adjusting the balance of specific frequency ranges in an audio signal.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>Short for equalization. The process of adjusting the relative level of
specific frequency ranges within an audio signal — boosting or cutting
bass, midrange, or treble. Used in recording, mixing, and mastering to
shape timbre, correct acoustic problems, and balance instruments in a
mix. Hardware and software EQ units are among the most fundamental
tools in audio production.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equalization_(audio)" target="_blank">1</a></span>
