      <span>See also: <a href="#mixing">mixing</a>, <a href="#timbre">timbre</a>, <a href="#effects">effects</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="technology" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="ewi">EWI</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[iː wiː]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Technology</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">Electronic wind instrument — a wind-controller that produces MIDI output.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>A wind-controller instrument played using breath and fingering
techniques similar to acoustic wind instruments, but producing MIDI
output that triggers a synthesizer rather than making acoustic sound
directly. The Akai EWI is the most widely used. Associated with
jazz-fusion players such as Michael Brecker and Bob Mintzer.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic_wind_instrument" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#midi">MIDI</a>, <a href="#synthesis">synthesis</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="form" data-importance="core">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="exposition">exposition</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[ˌɛkspəˈzɪʃən]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Form</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-core">Core</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">The opening section of a fugue or sonata form presenting the main themes.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>(1) In sonata form: the opening section in which the main themes are
introduced, typically moving from the home key to a contrasting key.
(2) In fugue: the opening section in which the subject is introduced
in each voice in turn.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exposition_(music)" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#sonata-form">sonata form</a>, <a href="#fugue">fugue</a>, <a href="#development">development</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="italian" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="falsetto">falsetto</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[fɒlˈsɛtoʊ]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Italian</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">A register above normal voice range produced by partial vibration of the vocal cords.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>Italian: "little false voice." A vocal register above the normal range
in which only part of the vocal cords vibrate, producing a lighter,
breathier tone. Common in countertenors, in pop singing (e.g., falsetto
passages in soul and R&B), and in yodelling. In classical pedagogy,
falsetto in men is related to but distinct from the head voice.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Falsetto" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#vocal-range">vocal range</a>, <a href="#tenor">tenor</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="figured-bass">figured bass</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[fˈɪɡəd beɪs]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">A Baroque notational shorthand in which numbers below a bass line indicate the harmonies to be played above it.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>A Baroque notation system in which numbers (figures) placed below a
bass line indicate the intervals to be played above it by the keyboard
continuo player. For example, a "6/3" indicates a first-inversion chord;
"7" indicates a seventh chord. The performer fills in appropriate
harmonies based on these figures, improvising within the conventions
of the style.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Figured_bass" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#basso-continuo">basso continuo</a>, <a href="#inversion">inversion</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="technology" data-importance="expert">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="fm-synthesis">FM synthesis</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[ɛf ɛm sˈɪnθəsɪs]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Technology</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-expert">Expert</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">Frequency modulation synthesis — generating complex timbres by modulating one oscillator&#x27;s frequency with another.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>A synthesis technique in which the frequency of one oscillator (the
carrier) is rapidly modulated by another oscillator (the modulator),
producing complex, harmonically rich timbres from simple sine waves.
Developed by John Chowning at Stanford and commercialized in the Yamaha
DX7 (1983), the best-selling synthesizer of all time. FM synthesis
produces characteristically bright, metallic, and bell-like sounds.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frequency_modulation_synthesis" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#subtractive-synthesis">subtractive synthesis</a>, <a href="#wavetable-synthesis">wavetable synthesis</a>, <a href="#synthesis">synthesis</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="form">form</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[fɔːɹm]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">The overall structure of a piece — how its sections are organized and relate to each other.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>The large-scale structural organization of a musical work — how its
sections are arranged, contrasted, and related. Common forms include
binary (AB), ternary (ABA), rondo (ABACABA), sonata form, theme and
variations, and strophic form. In popular music, common forms include
verse-chorus, 12-bar blues, and AABA (32-bar song form).</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musical_form" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#binary-form">binary form</a>, <a href="#ternary-form">ternary form</a>, <a href="#rondo-form">rondo form</a>, <a href="#sonata-form">sonata form</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="core">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="fugue">fugue</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[fjuːɡ]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-core">Core</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">A contrapuntal composition in which a theme (subject) is introduced and developed through imitation across voices.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>A contrapuntal composition structure in which a main theme (the subject)
is introduced alone in one voice, then taken up in imitation by
successive voices, each entering at a different pitch level. The
exposition is followed by episodes (passage work between subject entries)
and further subject statements. The fugue is the highest formal
achievement of strict counterpoint, exemplified by Bach's Well-Tempered
Clavier.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fugue" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#counterpoint">counterpoint</a>, <a href="#imitation">imitation</a>, <a href="#polyphony">polyphony</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="italian" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="glissando">glissando</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[ɡlɪˈsændoʊ]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Italian</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">A slide between two pitches.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>Italian/French: "gliding." A continuous slide in pitch between two
notes. On piano or harp, this involves running the finger rapidly
across adjacent keys or strings; on string instruments and trombone,
a true continuous glide is possible. Distinguished from portamento,
which is a lighter, more expressive slide in vocal and string
technique.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glissando" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#portamento">portamento</a>, <a href="#bent-notes">bent notes</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="technology" data-importance="expert">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="granular-synthesis">granular synthesis</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[ɡɹˈænjʊlər sˈɪnθəsɪs]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Technology</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-expert">Expert</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">A synthesis method that breaks sound into tiny fragments (grains) and reassembles them to create new textures.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>A digital synthesis technique in which a sound is broken into very
short fragments (grains, typically 1–100 ms) that can be independently
manipulated in pitch, duration, density, and spatial position, then
layered to form new textures. Developed theoretically by Iannis Xenakis
in the 1950s and first implemented on computer by Curtis Roads in the
1970s. Especially suited to evolving atmospheres, time-stretching, and
morphing sounds; also the underlying technology in most modern
time-stretch and pitch-shift algorithms.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granular_synthesis" target="_blank">1</a>, <a href="https://blog.native-instruments.com/granular-synthesis/" target="_blank">2</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#wavetable-synthesis">wavetable synthesis</a>, <a href="#subtractive-synthesis">subtractive synthesis</a>, <a href="#sampling">sampling</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="ground-bass">ground bass</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[ɡɹaʊnd beɪs]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">A repeating bass pattern over which variations are composed.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>A repeating bass line (or harmonic-bass pattern) over which a series
of variations is composed in the upper voices. A specific type of
ostinato. Central to Baroque music — Purcell's <strong>Dido's Lament</strong> and
Bach's <strong>Chaconne</strong> are classic examples. Related forms include the
passacaglia and chaconne.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ground_bass" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#ostinato">ostinato</a>, <a href="#basso-continuo">basso continuo</a>, <a href="#variation">variation</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="harmonic">harmonic</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[hɑːɹˈmɒnɪk]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">An overtone — a frequency that is a whole-number multiple of a fundamental pitch.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>A partial frequency that is a whole-number multiple of a fundamental
pitch. The first harmonic is the fundamental itself; the second harmonic
is an octave above; the third a perfect twelfth above, etc. The relative
strength of different harmonics determines timbre — what makes a violin
sound different from a flute on the same pitch. On string and wind
instruments, players can isolate harmonics as a technique (flageolet
tones, natural harmonics).</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmonic" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#timbre">timbre</a>, <a href="#acoustics">acoustics</a>, <a href="#overtone">overtone</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="harmonic-rhythm">harmonic rhythm</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[hɑːɹˈmɒnɪk ˈɹɪðəm]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">The rate at which chords change within a piece.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>The pace at which the underlying harmony changes — how frequently chord
changes occur. Slow harmonic rhythm (chords held for many beats) creates
a stable, spacious feel; fast harmonic rhythm (chords changing every
beat or more) creates tension and drive. A key analytical concept in
understanding a piece's pacing and energy.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmonic_rhythm" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#harmony">harmony</a>, <a href="#cadence">cadence</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="harmony" data-importance="core">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="hemiola">hemiola</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[ˌhɛmiˈoʊlə]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Harmony</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-core">Core</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">A rhythmic effect in which three beats in duple metre are temporarily felt as two in triple, or vice versa.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>A rhythmic pattern in which the regular metre is temporarily displaced
by grouping beats differently. In 6/8, for example, two bars of 3+3
eighth notes may be regrouped as three bars of 2+2, or vice versa.
Common at cadences in Baroque and Renaissance music, in Brahms, and
throughout African and Latin rhythmic traditions.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hemiola" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#syncopation">syncopation</a>, <a href="#polyrhythm">polyrhythm</a>, <a href="#metre">metre</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="heterophonic">heterophonic</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[ˌhɛtəɹəˈfɒnɪk]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">A texture in which multiple voices simultaneously perform variations of the same melody.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>A musical texture in which two or more voices perform the same basic
melody simultaneously but with slight variations — different
ornamentation, rhythmic placement, or embellishment. Common in many
world music traditions including gamelan, West African music, and
traditional folk musics. Distinct from polyphony (independent melodic
lines) and homophony (melody with harmonic support).</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heterophony" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#texture">texture</a>, <a href="#polyphony">polyphony</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="homophonic">homophonic</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[ˌhɒməˈfɒnɪk]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">A texture in which one voice carries the melody while others provide harmonic support.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>A musical texture in which one melodic voice is primary, supported by
accompanying voices that provide harmony without independent melodic
interest. The most common texture in Western popular and classical music
from the late Baroque onward. Distinguished from polyphony (independent
equal voices) and monophony (single voice with no accompaniment).</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homophony" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#texture">texture</a>, <a href="#polyphony">polyphony</a>, <a href="#monophonic">monophonic</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="idiophone">idiophone</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[ˈɪdiəfoʊn]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">An instrument that produces sound through the vibration of its own body.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>One of the four primary instrument categories in the Hornbostel-Sachs
classification system. Idiophones produce sound through the vibration
of the instrument's own body, without a stretched membrane, string, or
air column. Examples include xylophones, cymbals, bells, rattles,
castanets, and steel drums.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Idiophone" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#membranophone">membranophone</a>, <a href="#chordophone">chordophone</a>, <a href="#aerophone">aerophone</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="imitation">imitation</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[ˌɪmɪˈteɪʃən]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">The repetition of a melodic idea in a different voice shortly after its first appearance.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>A contrapuntal technique in which a melodic idea introduced in one
voice is taken up and repeated in another voice, typically at a
different pitch, shortly after the first voice. The basis of canonic
writing and fugue. Strict imitation preserves exact intervals; tonal
imitation adjusts them to stay within the key.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imitation_(music)" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#canon">canon</a>, <a href="#fugue">fugue</a>, <a href="#counterpoint">counterpoint</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="improvising">improvising</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[ˈɪmpɹəvaɪzɪŋ]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">Creating music spontaneously in performance, within a given harmonic or stylistic framework.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>The spontaneous creation of musical material in real time during
performance. Improvisation may be free (without predetermined
structure) or guided by a chord progression, mode, raga, or other
framework. Central to jazz, Indian classical music, flamenco, and
many other traditions. Distinct from interpretation of written music,
though the two overlap.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musical_improvisation" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#raga">raga</a>, <a href="#alap">alap</a>, <a href="#head">head</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="core">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="interval">interval</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[ˈɪntəvəl]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-core">Core</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">The pitch distance between two notes.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>The distance in pitch between two notes, measured in semitones and
named by their scale-degree distance. Basic intervals include unison,
second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, and octave, each further
qualified as major, minor, perfect, augmented, or diminished.
Intervals are the building blocks of melody, harmony, and counterpoint.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interval_(music)" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#semitone">semitone</a>, <a href="#consonance">consonance</a>, <a href="#dissonance">dissonance</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="harmony" data-importance="core">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="inversion">inversion</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[ɪnˈvɜːɹʒən]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Harmony</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-core">Core</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">(1) A chord with a note other than the root in the bass; (2) a melody flipped upside down.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>The term has two related meanings. (1) Chord inversion: a chord arranged
so that a note other than the root is in the lowest voice. First
inversion has the third in the bass; second inversion has the fifth.
(2) Melodic inversion: a melody restated with all intervals flipped
(ascending intervals become descending and vice versa). Both uses are
important in counterpoint and tonal harmony.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inversion_(music)" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#retrograde">retrograde</a>, <a href="#root-position">root position</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="key-change">key change</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[kiː tʃeɪndʒ]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">A shift from one tonal center to another within a piece.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>A shift from one key (tonal center) to another at some point within
a piece. May be gradual (through pivot chords or chromatic voice
leading) or abrupt. A common device in popular music is the
"truck driver's modulation" — an upward shift by a semitone or whole
tone near the end of a song.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modulation_(music)" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#modulation-in-music">modulation</a>, <a href="#tonality">tonality</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="layering">layering</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[lˈeɪərɪŋ]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">Building up a texture by combining multiple simultaneous parts or sounds.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>The compositional and production technique of combining multiple
simultaneous musical parts, samples, or synthesized sounds to create a
richer or more complex texture. In production, layers may include
multiple harmony parts, doubled melody lines, stacked synth patches,
or blended drum sounds.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arrangement_(music)" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#texture">texture</a>, <a href="#overdubbing">overdubbing</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="leading-note">leading note</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[lˈiːdɪŋ noʊt]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">The seventh scale degree, a half step below the tonic, with strong upward tendency.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>The seventh degree of the major scale — a semitone below the tonic —
which has a strong tendency to resolve upward to the tonic. Its pull
toward resolution is central to tonal harmony and voice leading. In
natural minor, the seventh degree is a whole tone below the tonic (the
subtonic); raising it to a semitone creates the harmonic minor scale.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leading-tone" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#scale-degrees">scale degrees</a>, <a href="#tonality">tonality</a>, <a href="#dominant">dominant</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="homograph" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="lead-voice-sheet">lead (voice/sheet)</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[liːd]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Homograph</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">The primary melody or melodic voice.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>In music, "lead" (rhymes with "feed") refers to the primary melodic line
or voice. A lead sheet is a simplified score showing melody, chord
symbols, and lyrics. The lead voice in a choir or ensemble carries the
main melody. Distinct from lead (the metal, rhyming with "bed").</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lead_sheet" target="_blank">1</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="technology" data-importance="expert">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="lfo">LFO</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[ɛl ɛf oʊ]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Technology</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-expert">Expert</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">Low-frequency oscillator — a slow-cycling modulation source in a synthesizer.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>An oscillator in a synthesizer that operates at very low frequencies
(typically below 20 Hz, below the threshold of hearing) and is used to
modulate other parameters rhythmically — most commonly pitch (producing
vibrato), amplitude (producing tremolo), or filter cutoff. LFO rate
determines the speed of the modulation; LFO depth determines its amount.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Low-frequency_oscillation" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#vibrato">vibrato</a>, <a href="#tremolo">tremolo</a>, <a href="#synthesis">synthesis</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="italian" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="libretto">libretto</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[lɪˈbɹɛtoʊ]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Italian</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">The text of an opera, oratorio, or other large-scale vocal work.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>Italian: "little book." The words — including sung text and stage
directions — of an opera, operetta, oratorio, or musical. The librettist
works in collaboration with the composer. Notable librettist-composer
partnerships include da Ponte and Mozart, and Boito and Verdi.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Libretto" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#aria">aria</a>, <a href="#recitative">recitative</a>, <a href="#opera">opera</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="loop">loop</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[luːp]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">A segment of audio edited to repeat seamlessly when played end to end.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>A short segment of audio that has been edited so its end connects
smoothly to its beginning, allowing seamless continuous repetition.
Loops are foundational to DAW-based production, electronic dance music,
and hip-hop. May be pre-recorded (sample loops) or created live using
loop pedals or DAW features.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loop_(music)" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#ostinato">ostinato</a>, <a href="#sampling">sampling</a>, <a href="#daw">DAW</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="non-western" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="maqam">maqam</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[məˈkɑːm]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Non-Western</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">A melodic mode in Arabic and Middle Eastern music, combining scale, characteristic phrases, and expressive character.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>In Arabic and broader Middle Eastern music traditions, a maqam (plural:
maqamat) is a melodic framework that goes beyond a simple scale to
include characteristic melodic phrases, ornaments, starting and ending
notes, and emotional associations. Hundreds of maqamat exist across the
region, many using intervals smaller than a semitone.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maqam" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#microtone">microtone</a>, <a href="#mode-modal">mode/modal</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="italian" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="melisma">melisma</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[məˈlɪzmə]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Italian</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">The singing of multiple notes on a single syllable.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>A passage in which a single syllable of text is sung across several
notes. Melisma is characteristic of Gregorian chant, Renaissance
polyphony, Arabic maqam, gospel, and R&B/soul music. The opposite of
syllabic singing, in which each syllable receives a single note.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melisma" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#syllabic">syllabic</a>, <a href="#ornamentation">ornamentation</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="metre">metre</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[mˈiːtəɹ]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">The recurring pattern of strong and weak beats that organizes rhythm in music.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>The organized pattern of strong and weak beats that provides a rhythmic
framework for music. Duple metre groups beats in twos (2/4, 4/4);
triple metre in threes (3/4, 3/8); compound metre divides each beat
into three equal parts (6/8, 9/8, 12/8). Irregular or mixed metres use
non-standard groupings (5/4, 7/8, etc.).</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metre_(music)" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#time-signature">time signature</a>, <a href="#syncopation">syncopation</a>, <a href="#hemiola">hemiola</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="microtone">microtone</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[ˈmaɪkɹətoʊn]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">Any interval smaller than a semitone.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>Any musical interval smaller than a semitone — the smallest step in
the standard Western chromatic scale. Includes quarter-tones (half a
semitone), third-tones, and the continuous pitch inflections found in
Arabic maqam, Indian raga, blues, and many other traditions. Also used
in 20th- and 21st-century composed music (Partch, Scelsi, Haas).</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microtone" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#quarter-tones">quarter-tones</a>, <a href="#temperament">temperament</a>, <a href="#maqam">maqam</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="technology" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="midi">MIDI</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[ˈmɪdi]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Technology</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">Musical Instrument Digital Interface — a protocol for communication between electronic instruments and computers.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>A technical standard (introduced 1983) that allows electronic musical
instruments, computers, and controllers to communicate and synchronize.
MIDI transmits performance data (note on/off, velocity, pitch bend,
etc.) rather than audio signals. A MIDI file contains instructions, not
sound; the actual sound depends on the playback device or software.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MIDI" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#midi-controller">MIDI controller</a>, <a href="#daw">DAW</a>, <a href="#sequencer">sequencer</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="midi-controller">MIDI controller</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[ˈmɪdi kənˈtɹoʊlər]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">A hardware or software device that sends MIDI data to control electronic instruments.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>Any device that generates and transmits MIDI data — note messages,
control changes, pitch bend, etc. — to trigger and control MIDI-capable
instruments and software. Includes keyboard controllers, drum pads,
wind controllers (EWI), and software-based controllers. Does not
produce sound itself; it controls sound sources.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MIDI_controller" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#midi">MIDI</a>, <a href="#ewi">EWI</a>, <a href="#daw">DAW</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="harmony" data-importance="core">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="minuet">minuet</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[ˌmɪnjuˈɛt]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Harmony</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-core">Core</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">A stately French dance in triple metre; also a standard movement in Classical symphonies.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>A French court dance in moderate triple metre, originating in the
17th century. As an abstract form, the minuet became the standard third
movement of Classical symphonies, sonatas, and chamber works, typically
in A–B–A form (minuet–trio–minuet). Beethoven replaced it with the
faster scherzo.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minuet" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#scherzo">scherzo</a>, <a href="#ternary-form">ternary form</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="mixing">mixing</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[mˈɪksɪŋ]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">Combining and balancing multi-track recordings into a final stereo or surround output.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>The process of combining separately recorded tracks into a cohesive
final product by adjusting relative levels, panning, EQ, dynamics, and
effects. Mixing follows tracking (recording) and precedes mastering.
The goal is a balanced, clear result in which all elements occupy
appropriate space in the frequency spectrum and stereo field.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Audio_mixing" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#mastering">mastering</a>, <a href="#daw">DAW</a>, <a href="#eq">EQ</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="modulation-in-music">modulation (in music)</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[ˌmɒdjʊˈleɪʃən]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">A change of key within a piece of music.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>The process of moving from one key (tonal center) to another within a
piece. Common modulation techniques include pivot chord modulation
(using a chord common to both keys), chromatic modulation (using a
chromatic alteration to shift to the new key), and direct (abrupt) key
change. Modulation creates tonal variety and dramatic effect.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modulation_(music)" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#key-change">key change</a>, <a href="#tonality">tonality</a>, <a href="#pivot-chord">pivot chord</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="core">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="motif">motif</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[moʊˈtiːf]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-core">Core</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">A short, distinctive musical idea — melodic, rhythmic, or harmonic — used as a building block.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>A brief, distinctive musical unit — typically just a few notes — that
recurs and is developed throughout a piece. Motifs may be melodic,
rhythmic, or harmonic. The opening four notes of Beethoven's Fifth
Symphony are the most famous example. Through development, inversion,
augmentation, and fragmentation, a motif can generate large amounts of
material.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motif_(music)" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#sequence">sequence</a>, <a href="#development">development</a>, <a href="#leitmotif">leitmotif</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="non-tonal">non-tonal</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[nɒn toʊnəl]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">Music that does not organize pitch around a central tonic.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>Music that does not establish or imply a tonal center. Encompasses both
atonal music (actively avoiding tonal hierarchies, as in Schoenberg's
free atonality) and other non-tonal systems such as twelve-tone
serialism. Different from modal music, which does organize around a
center but outside major/minor tonality.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atonality" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#atonal">atonal</a>, <a href="#12-note-techniques">12-note techniques</a>, <a href="#tonality">tonality</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="notation">notation</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[noʊˈteɪʃən]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">Any system of symbols used to represent music visually.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>Any system of written symbols used to represent music for the purposes
of performance or analysis. Western staff notation uses a five-line
staff, noteheads, clefs, key signatures, and time signatures. Other
systems include tablature, graphic scores, lead sheets with chord
symbols, and various non-Western notations.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musical_notation" target="_blank">1</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="italian" data-importance="core">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="ostinato">ostinato</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[ˌɒstɪˈnɑːtoʊ]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Italian</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-core">Core</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">A persistently repeated melodic, rhythmic, or harmonic pattern.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>Italian: "obstinate." A short musical pattern — melodic, rhythmic, or
harmonic — that repeats persistently throughout a piece or section.
A ground bass is a specific type of harmonic/bass ostinato. Ostinato is
fundamental to minimalist music, African drumming, and many popular music
styles.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ostinato" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#ground-bass">ground bass</a>, <a href="#riff">riff</a>, <a href="#pedal-tone">pedal tone</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="overdubbing">overdubbing</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[ˌoʊvəɹdˈʌbɪŋ]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">Recording additional tracks onto an existing recording to layer multiple performances.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>A recording technique in which new audio material is recorded onto
separate tracks while listening to previously recorded material through
headphones. Allows a single performer to build up complex textures by
layering multiple performances, or a band to record instruments
separately. Pioneered in the 1940s by Les Paul.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overdubbing" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#daw">DAW</a>, <a href="#tracking">tracking</a>, <a href="#layering">layering</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="passing-tone">passing tone</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[pˈæsɪŋ toʊn]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">A non-chord tone that moves by step between two chord tones.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>A non-chord tone that fills in the stepwise space between two chord
tones, approached and left by step in the same direction. A diatonic
passing tone stays within the key; a chromatic passing tone uses a
note from outside the key to fill a whole-step gap. Fundamental to
melodic writing and counterpoint.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonchord_tone" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#suspensions">suspensions</a>, <a href="#appoggiatura">appoggiatura</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="pedal-tone">pedal tone</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[pˈɛdəl toʊn]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">A sustained or repeated note (usually in the bass) held while harmonies change above it.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>A sustained or repeated pitch — most commonly in the bass — held while
the harmony above it changes. Named after the organ pedal, which can
sustain bass notes independently of the manuals. A tonic pedal reinforces
the home key; a dominant pedal creates tension before a cadence. Also
used in upper voices (an inverted pedal).</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pedal_point" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#drone">drone</a>, <a href="#basso-continuo">basso continuo</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="non-western" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="pelog">pelog</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[ˈpeɪlɒɡ]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Non-Western</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">One of the two main tuning systems in Javanese and Balinese gamelan music.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>One of the two principal scales used in Javanese and Balinese gamelan
music, typically containing seven unequal pitches per octave, of which
five are used in any given piece. Characterized by its large and small
intervals, pelog has a more tense, formal character compared to the
more open-sounding slendro.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%A9log" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#slendro">slendro</a>, <a href="#gamelan">gamelan</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="harmony" data-importance="core">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="pentatonic">pentatonic</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[ˌpɛntəˈtɒnɪk]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Harmony</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-core">Core</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">A five-note scale, common across many world music traditions.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>A scale consisting of five pitches per octave. The major pentatonic
(e.g., C–D–E–G–A) and minor pentatonic (e.g., A–C–D–E–G) are the most
common forms and appear in folk, blues, rock, jazz, and many world
music traditions. The blues scale adds a flattened fifth to the minor
pentatonic.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pentatonic_scale" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#blues-scale">blues scale</a>, <a href="#mode-modal">mode/modal</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="phasing">phasing</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[fˈeɪzɪŋ]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">A compositional technique in which the same pattern in two voices gradually moves out of synchronisation.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>A minimalist compositional technique, pioneered by Steve Reich, in which
the same repeating pattern is played simultaneously by two performers
or voices at very slightly different tempos. As the patterns slowly fall
out of sync, new composite rhythmic and melodic patterns emerge, then
gradually re-align. Key works include Reich's <strong>Piano Phase</strong> (1967) and
<strong>Drumming</strong> (1971).</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phase_music" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#polyrhythm">polyrhythm</a>, <a href="#ostinato">ostinato</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="italian" data-importance="core">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="pizzicato">pizzicato</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[ˌpɪtsɪˈkɑːtoʊ]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Italian</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-core">Core</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">Plucking the strings of a bowed instrument with the fingers.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>Italian: "pinched." A technique for bowed string instruments in which
the strings are plucked with the fingers rather than bowed, producing
a dry, percussive tone. Indicated in scores by the abbreviation pizz.;
arco or con arco marks the return to bowing.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pizzicato" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#arco">arco</a>, <a href="#timbre">timbre</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="plagal-cadence">plagal cadence</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[plˈeɪɡəl kˈeɪdəns]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">A cadence moving from IV to I, often called the &quot;Amen&quot; cadence.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>A cadential formula in which the subdominant chord (IV) resolves to the
tonic (I). Produces a softer, more settled effect than the authentic
(V–I) cadence. Frequently used at the word "Amen" in hymns and choral
music, hence its informal name.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cadence_(music)" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#authentic-perfect-cadence">authentic cadence</a>, <a href="#cadence">cadence</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="core">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="polyphony">polyphony</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[pəlˈɪfəni]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-core">Core</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">A texture of two or more independent melodic lines sounding simultaneously.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>A musical texture in which two or more independent melodic voices sound
simultaneously, each with its own rhythmic and melodic identity.
Distinguished from homophony (melody with chordal accompaniment) and
monophony (single melody alone). The Renaissance motet and Baroque
fugue represent the highest development of Western polyphonic writing.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polyphony" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#counterpoint">counterpoint</a>, <a href="#fugue">fugue</a>, <a href="#texture">texture</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="harmony" data-importance="core">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="polyrhythm">polyrhythm</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[ˈpɒlɪɹɪðəm]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Harmony</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-core">Core</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">Two or more different rhythmic patterns performed simultaneously.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>The simultaneous use of two or more conflicting rhythmic patterns. A
common example is three against two (3:2), in which one voice plays
three equal beats while another plays two over the same duration.
Polyrhythm is central to West African music, Afro-Cuban music, and
appears throughout jazz, contemporary classical, and global traditions.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polyrhythm" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#hemiola">hemiola</a>, <a href="#cross-rhythms">cross rhythms</a>, <a href="#metre">metre</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="italian" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="portamento">portamento</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[ˌpɔːɹtəˈmɛntoʊ]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Italian</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">A smooth, expressive slide between two notes.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>Italian: "carrying." A smooth, continuous glide from one pitch to
another, used expressively in vocal and string performance. Differs from
glissando in being a more subtle, expressive gesture rather than a rapid
technical slide through all intermediate pitches. Also a feature in
synthesizers, where portamento (or glide) time determines how quickly
the pitch shifts between played notes.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portamento" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#glissando">glissando</a>, <a href="#legato">legato</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="quantization">quantization</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[ˌkwɒntɪˈzeɪʃən]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">Snapping recorded notes to the nearest rhythmic grid position in a DAW.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>In digital music production, quantization is the process of adjusting
the timing of recorded MIDI notes so they align precisely to a rhythmic
grid (e.g., eighth notes or sixteenth notes). It corrects timing
imprecision and can impose machine-like regularity or, when applied
partially, preserve a degree of human feel. Distinct from audio
quantization (bit depth), though the term is shared.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantization_(music)" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#midi">MIDI</a>, <a href="#daw">DAW</a>, <a href="#sequencer">sequencer</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="quarter-tones">quarter-tones</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[kwˈɔːɹtəɹ toʊnz]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">Intervals half the size of a semitone, used in microtonal music and many non-Western traditions.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>An interval equal to half a semitone — one quarter of a whole tone.
Quarter-tones fall between the notes of the standard Western chromatic
scale and cannot be played on a fixed-pitch instrument such as a piano
without retuning. Central to Arabic maqam music, used in some
contemporary classical compositions (e.g., Bartók, Scelsi), and
producible on fretless string instruments, voice, and certain winds.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quarter_tone" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#microtone">microtone</a>, <a href="#maqam">maqam</a>, <a href="#temperament">temperament</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="non-western" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="raga">raga</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[ˈɹɑːɡə]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Non-Western</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">A melodic framework in Indian classical music combining scale, characteristic phrases, and emotional character.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>In Indian classical music, a raga is a melodic framework that specifies
a set of pitches, characteristic ascending and descending patterns,
ornaments, important notes, and an associated emotional quality (rasa)
and time of performance. A raga is not simply a scale but a complete
guide to melodic improvisation within a tradition.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raga" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#alap">alap</a>, <a href="#maqam">maqam</a>, <a href="#mode-modal">mode/modal</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="form" data-importance="core">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="recapitulation">recapitulation</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[ˌɹiːkəˌpɪtʃuˈleɪʃən]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Form</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-core">Core</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">The third section of sonata form, restating the exposition&#x27;s themes in the home key.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>The third and final main section of sonata form, in which the themes
of the exposition are restated — usually both in the home key, resolving
the tonal tension established by the exposition's modulation. The
recapitulation follows the development section.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recapitulation_(music)" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#sonata-form">sonata form</a>, <a href="#exposition">exposition</a>, <a href="#development">development</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="italian" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="recitative">recitative</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[ˌɹɛsɪtəˈtiːv]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Italian</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">A vocal style that follows speech rhythms, used in opera and oratorio to advance the narrative.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>A style of vocal writing that imitates the rhythms and inflections of
natural speech, used in opera, oratorio, and cantata to narrate events
and advance the plot between more formally structured arias. Recitativo
secco ("dry recitative") is accompanied only by sparse keyboard chords;
recitativo accompagnato (or stromentato) is accompanied by the full
orchestra.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recitative" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#aria">aria</a>, <a href="#cantata">cantata</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="relative-major-minor">relative (major/minor)</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[ˈɹɛlətɪv]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">A major and minor key sharing the same key signature.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>A relative key is a major or minor key that shares the same key
signature as another key. C major and A minor are relative keys — they
share no sharps or flats, but have different tonics and different
characteristic harmonies. Every major key has a relative minor a minor
third below it.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Relative_key" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#key-change">key change</a>, <a href="#tonality">tonality</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="harmony" data-importance="core">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="retrograde">retrograde</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[ˈɹɛtɹəɡɹeɪd]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Harmony</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-core">Core</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">A theme played backwards — the last note becomes first.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>A compositional technique in which a melodic line or row is stated
in reverse order. Used in canonic writing, twelve-tone technique, and
as a developmental device. Retrograde inversion applies both reversal
and mirror-image pitch transformation simultaneously.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retrograde_(music)" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#retrograde-inversion">retrograde inversion</a>, <a href="#inversion">inversion</a>, <a href="#12-note-techniques">12-note techniques</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="reverb">reverb</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[ˈɹiːvɜːɹb]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">The persistence of sound caused by multiple reflections in a space, decaying gradually.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>The persistence of sound after its source has stopped, caused by
multiple reflections of sound waves from surfaces in a space. In
music production, reverb is applied as an audio effect — using echo
chambers, plate or spring reverb hardware, or digital algorithms — to
give sounds a sense of space and environment. Distinct from delay
(echo), in which individual reflections are heard separately; in
reverb, reflections blend into a continuous wash.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reverberation" target="_blank">1</a>, <a href="https://splice.com/blog/what-is-reverb/" target="_blank">2</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#delay">delay</a>, <a href="#wet-dry-signal">wet/dry signal</a>, <a href="#effects">effects</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="riff">riff</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[ɹɪf]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">A short, repeating melodic or rhythmic figure, especially in jazz, blues, and rock.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>A short, memorable melodic or rhythmic pattern that recurs throughout a
piece, often as an accompaniment or hook. Central to jazz, blues, rock,
and funk — the guitar riff is a defining element of rock music, while
horn riffs underpin big band swing. Related to ostinato but typically
more groove-oriented.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riff" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#ostinato">ostinato</a>, <a href="#motif">motif</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="rondo-form">rondo form</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[ˈɹɒndoʊ fɔːɹm]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">A form in which a main theme (A) alternates with contrasting episodes: ABACA or ABACABA.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>A musical form built around a recurring main theme (the refrain, A)
that alternates with contrasting episodes (B, C, etc.). Common patterns
include ABACA (five-part) and ABACABA (seven-part). The refrain always
returns in the tonic key; episodes typically move to related keys. Rondo
was particularly popular as a final movement in Classical concerti and
sonatas. Emerged from the French Baroque keyboard rondeau.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rondo" target="_blank">1</a>, <a href="https://www.britannica.com/art/rondo" target="_blank">2</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#sonata-form">sonata form</a>, <a href="#binary-form">binary form</a>, <a href="#ternary-form">ternary form</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="italian" data-importance="core">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="rubato">rubato</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[ɹuːˈbɑːtoʊ]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Italian</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-core">Core</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">Flexible tempo; slight speeding up and slowing down for expressive effect.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>Italian: "robbed time." A direction to perform with slight flexibility of
tempo for expressive purposes, speeding up or slowing down phrases as
the music and feeling demand. Common in Romantic music and jazz
ballads. Not random: effective rubato involves subtle give-and-take
that enhances rather than distorts the musical line.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tempo_rubato" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#tempo">tempo</a>, <a href="#accelerando">accelerando</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="sampling">sampling</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[sˈæmplɪŋ]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">Reusing a portion of an existing recording in a new composition.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>The practice of taking a segment (sample) of a recorded sound and
incorporating it into a new piece. Samples may be looped, pitch-shifted,
time-stretched, layered, or otherwise manipulated. Sampling is
foundational to hip-hop, electronic, and dance music production.
Legally, sampling of commercial recordings generally requires licensing.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sampling_(music)" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#loop">loop</a>, <a href="#daw">DAW</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="italian" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="scherzo">scherzo</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[skˈɛɹtsoʊ]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Italian</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">A lively, often humorous movement, typically in triple metre, common in Classical and Romantic symphonies.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>Italian for "joke." A fast, energetic movement in triple metre that
replaced the minuet as the third movement of the Classical symphony,
most notably in the works of Beethoven. Scherzos are characterized by
rhythmic drive, sudden dynamic contrasts, and often playful or
surprising character. The form is typically A–B–A (scherzo–trio–scherzo).</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scherzo" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#minuet">minuet</a>, <a href="#ternary-form">ternary form</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="sequence">sequence</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[sˈiːkwəns]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">Immediate repetition of a melodic or harmonic pattern at a different pitch level.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>A compositional device in which a melodic or harmonic pattern is
repeated immediately at a higher or lower pitch. A tonal sequence adjusts
intervals to stay within the key; a real sequence preserves exact
interval sizes regardless of key. Sequences are a primary tool for
extending and developing musical ideas.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sequence_(music)" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#motif">motif</a>, <a href="#development">development</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="italian" data-importance="core">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="sforzando">sforzando</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[sfɔːɹtsˈændoʊ]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Italian</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-core">Core</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">A sudden, strong accent on a single note or chord.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>Italian: "forcing." A dynamic marking indicating that a single note or
chord should be played with a sudden, sharp accent, significantly louder
than the surrounding passage. Abbreviated sfz or sf. Related to
forzando (fz), which carries a similar meaning.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynamics_(music)" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#dynamics">dynamics</a>, <a href="#accent">accent</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="non-western" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="slendro">slendro</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[ˈslɛndɹoʊ]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Non-Western</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">One of the two main tuning systems in Javanese and Balinese gamelan, with five roughly equal pitches per octave.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>One of the two principal scales of Javanese and Balinese gamelan, with
five tones per octave spaced in roughly equal intervals. It has a more
open, flowing character than pelog. The exact tuning varies between
different gamelan sets, as each instrument is tuned to match others
within the same gamelan rather than to an external standard.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sl%C3%A9ndro" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#pelog">pelog</a>, <a href="#gamelan">gamelan</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="italian" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="solf-ge">solfège</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[ˈsɒlfɛʒ]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Italian</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">A method of assigning syllables (do, re, mi…) to scale degrees to aid sight-singing.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>A pedagogical system for ear training and sight-singing in which each
degree of the scale is assigned a syllable: do, re, mi, fa, sol, la,
