ti (or si). In movable-do systems, do always represents the tonic
regardless of key; in fixed-do systems (common in France and Italy), do
always represents C. Solfège is foundational to Gordon's Music Learning
Theory (MLT) through the use of tonal patterns.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solf%C3%A8ge" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#scale-degrees">scale degrees</a>, <a href="#aural-perception">aural perception</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="italian" data-importance="core">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="sonata">sonata</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[səˈnɑːtə]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Italian</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-core">Core</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">A multi-movement instrumental work, typically for one or two instruments.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>Italian: "sounded piece." A multi-movement instrumental composition,
typically for a solo instrument (piano sonata) or a solo instrument
with piano accompaniment. The Classical sonata typically has three or
four movements in contrasting tempos and keys. The term has evolved
considerably across history; Baroque sonatas differ substantially
from Classical and Romantic ones.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonata" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#sonata-form">sonata form</a>, <a href="#binary-form">binary form</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="sonata-form">sonata form</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[səˈnɑːtə fɔːɹm]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">A large-scale form in three sections: exposition, development, and recapitulation.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>The primary formal structure of the first movement (and sometimes other
movements) of Classical-era sonatas, symphonies, and chamber works.
Consists of three main sections: the exposition (presenting two or more
contrasting themes in different keys), the development (fragmenting and
transforming that material through varied keys), and the recapitulation
(restating the exposition with both themes in the home key). Often
preceded by a slow introduction and followed by a coda.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonata_form" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#exposition">exposition</a>, <a href="#development">development</a>, <a href="#recapitulation">recapitulation</a>, <a href="#coda">coda</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="vocal" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="soprano">soprano</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[səˈpɹɑːnoʊ]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Vocal</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">The highest standard singing voice type.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>The highest standard voice type, typically ranging from C4 to C6 or
higher depending on the type (lyric, dramatic, coloratura). In choral
writing, the soprano carries the top voice. In opera, the soprano is
frequently cast as the heroine.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soprano" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#tenor">tenor</a>, <a href="#alto">alto</a>, <a href="#tessitura">tessitura</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="italian" data-importance="core">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="staccato">staccato</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[stəkˈɑːtoʊ]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Italian</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-core">Core</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">A direction to play notes short and detached.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>Italian: "detached." An articulation marking directing the performer to
shorten the duration of a note, creating separation between it and the
following note. Notated by a dot placed above or below the note head.
The opposite of legato (smooth and connected).</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Staccato" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#articulation">articulation</a>, <a href="#legato">legato</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="italian" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="stringendo">stringendo</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[stɹɪnˈdʒɛndoʊ]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Italian</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">Pressing forward; urgently accelerating.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>Italian: "pressing, squeezing." A direction to accelerate urgently, with
mounting intensity. Often associated with a climactic passage. Similar
to accelerando but with a stronger connotation of dramatic urgency.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Italian_musical_terms_used_in_English" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#accelerando">accelerando</a>, <a href="#tempo">tempo</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="harmony" data-importance="core">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="strophic-form">strophic form</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[ˈstɹɒfɪk fɔːɹm]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Harmony</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-core">Core</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">A song structure in which the same music is repeated for each verse.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>A song structure in which the same (or nearly the same) music is used
for each stanza or verse of the text. Simple and widely used in folk
song, hymns, and early art song. Distinguished from through-composed
form, in which new music is written for each section.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strophic_form" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#through-composed">through-composed</a>, <a href="#verse-chorus-structure">verse-chorus structure</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="expert">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="subtractive-synthesis">subtractive synthesis</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[səbtrˈæktɪv sˈɪnθəsɪs]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-expert">Expert</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">Synthesis that starts with a harmonically rich waveform and removes frequencies using filters.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>A method of sound synthesis that begins with an oscillator producing a
harmonically complex waveform (sawtooth, square, or noise) and then uses
filters to attenuate or remove certain frequencies, shaping the timbre of
the result. The most common synthesis method in classic analog
synthesizers (Moog, Roland, etc.). The filter cutoff frequency and
resonance are the primary timbral controls.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subtractive_synthesis" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#fm-synthesis">FM synthesis</a>, <a href="#wavetable-synthesis">wavetable synthesis</a>, <a href="#filter">filter</a>, <a href="#oscillator">oscillator</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="italian" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="sul-ponticello">sul ponticello</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[sʊl ˌpɒntɪˈtʃɛloʊ]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Italian</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">Bowing near the bridge of a string instrument to produce a glassy, nasal tone.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>Italian: "on the little bridge." A direction for string players to bow
close to the bridge, producing a bright, glassy, or nasal tone with
prominent upper harmonics. The opposite is sul tasto (bowing over the
fingerboard), which produces a softer, flutier sound.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sul_ponticello" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#timbre">timbre</a>, <a href="#arco">arco</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="suspensions">suspensions</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[səspˈɛnʃənz]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">Non-chord tones held over from a previous chord that resolve by step.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>A suspension occurs when a note from a previous chord is held or
repeated while the harmony changes beneath it, creating a dissonance
that then resolves by step (usually downward) to a chord tone. Labeled
by the interval numbers of the dissonance and resolution (e.g., 4–3
or 7–6). A fundamental technique in tonal voice leading, particularly
prominent in Renaissance and Baroque counterpoint.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suspension_(music)" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#appoggiatura">appoggiatura</a>, <a href="#consonance">consonance</a>, <a href="#dissonance">dissonance</a>, <a href="#resolution">resolution</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="harmony" data-importance="core">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="syncopation">syncopation</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[ˌsɪŋkəpˈeɪʃən]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Harmony</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-core">Core</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">Placing rhythmic accents on normally weak beats or between beats.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>A rhythmic technique in which accents fall on beats or parts of beats
that are normally unaccented, displacing the expected rhythmic emphasis.
Syncopation creates energy, forward drive, and rhythmic tension. It is
central to jazz, funk, Latin, and African music, and appears throughout
Western art music as well.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syncopation" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#rhythm">rhythm</a>, <a href="#hemiola">hemiola</a>, <a href="#metric-displacement">metric displacement</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="synthesis">synthesis</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[sˈɪnθəsɪs]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">The generation of sound using electronic hardware or software.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>The production of audio signals through electronic means rather than
acoustic instrument performance. The major synthesis methods include
subtractive, additive, FM (frequency modulation), wavetable, granular,
physical modelling, and sample-based synthesis, each differing in how
they generate and shape waveforms.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sound_synthesis" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#subtractive-synthesis">subtractive synthesis</a>, <a href="#fm-synthesis">FM synthesis</a>, <a href="#wavetable-synthesis">wavetable synthesis</a>, <a href="#granular-synthesis">granular synthesis</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="temperament">temperament</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[tˈɛmpəɹəmənt]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">A tuning system that adjusts pure intervals to allow playing in multiple keys.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>A system of tuning in which the mathematically pure intervals of just
intonation are slightly adjusted so that an instrument can play
acceptably in all keys. Equal temperament — the standard system today —
divides the octave into twelve equal semitones, meaning every key sounds
equally (slightly) out of tune. Earlier systems such as meantone and
well temperament made some keys purer at the expense of others.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musical_temperament" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#tuning">tuning</a>, <a href="#microtone">microtone</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="core">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="tempo">tempo</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[tˈɛmpoʊ]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-core">Core</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">The speed of the beat, measured in beats per minute (BPM).</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>The rate at which a piece of music is performed, typically measured in
beats per minute (BPM). Tempo may be indicated by Italian terms (adagio,
allegro, presto), by metronome markings, or by descriptive words. It can
be fixed or variable (as in rubato), and changes of tempo within a piece
may be gradual (accelerando, ritardando) or sudden.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tempo" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#accelerando">accelerando</a>, <a href="#rubato">rubato</a>, <a href="#pulse">pulse</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="tenor">tenor</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[tˈɛnəɹ]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">The highest standard adult male singing voice.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>The highest of the standard adult male voice types, sitting above
baritone and bass. The tenor range typically spans from C3 to C5 (or
higher in falsetto). In choral writing, the tenor part occupies the
second-lowest voice. Notable tenor voice types include lyric, dramatic,
and heldentenor.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tenor" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#soprano">soprano</a>, <a href="#baritone">baritone</a>, <a href="#tessitura">tessitura</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="italian" data-importance="core">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="tenuto">tenuto</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[tɛˈnjuːtoʊ]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Italian</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-core">Core</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">Hold the note for its full value; often with slight emphasis.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>Italian: "held." An articulation marking indicating that a note should
be held for its full value — or slightly longer — and given a gentle
emphasis. Notated by a short horizontal line above or below the notehead.
Distinct from staccato (short) and accent (forceful).</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tenuto" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#articulation">articulation</a>, <a href="#legato">legato</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="ternary-form">ternary form</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[tˈɜːɹnəɹi fɔːɹm]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">A three-part musical structure: A–B–A.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>A musical form consisting of three sections: an opening section (A), a
contrasting middle section (B), and a return of the opening section (A).
The return may be exact or varied. Ternary form is among the most common
forms in Western music, found in da capo arias, many classical minuets,
and popular song structures. Distinguished from binary form (A–B) by the
return of the opening material.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ternary_form" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#binary-form">binary form</a>, <a href="#rondo-form">rondo form</a>, <a href="#sonata-form">sonata form</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="vocal" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="tessitura">tessitura</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[ˌtɛsɪˈtjʊəɹə]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Vocal</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">The range within which a voice or instrument most comfortably and characteristically sits.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>The general pitch range in which a vocal part or instrument most
frequently lies, as distinct from its absolute upper and lower limits.
A part may technically fall within a voice's total range but still be
poorly written if the tessitura sits too high or too low for comfortable
sustained performance. The term comes from the Italian for "texture."</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tessitura" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#vocal-range">vocal range</a>, <a href="#tenor">tenor</a>, <a href="#soprano">soprano</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="core">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="texture">texture</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[tˈɛkstʃəɹ]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-core">Core</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">The way melodic, rhythmic, and harmonic elements are combined in a piece.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>The overall character of a piece as determined by how its voices or
parts interact. The primary texture types are monophonic (single melody
with no accompaniment), homophonic (melody with chordal support),
polyphonic (two or more independent melodic lines), and heterophonic
(simultaneous variations of the same melody). Texture is one of the
primary musical elements alongside melody, rhythm, harmony, timbre, and
dynamics.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musical_texture" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#homophonic">homophonic</a>, <a href="#polyphony">polyphony</a>, <a href="#monophonic">monophonic</a>, <a href="#heterophonic">heterophonic</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="through-composed">through-composed</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[θɹuː kəmpˈoʊzd]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">A form in which new music is written for each section, with no large-scale repetition.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>A compositional structure in which each section of a piece uses new
musical material rather than repeating earlier sections. Contrasts with
forms built on repetition such as strophic form, binary, ternary, or
rondo. Through-composed pieces follow the dramatic or textual content
freely without returning to previous material, common in lieder (art
song) and opera.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Through-composed_music" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#strophic-form">strophic form</a>, <a href="#binary-form">binary form</a>, <a href="#rondo-form">rondo form</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="italian" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="tierce-de-picardie">tierce de Picardie</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[tjɛɹs də pɪkɑːɹˈdiː]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Italian</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">Ending a minor-key piece on a major tonic chord.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>A technique in which a piece or section written in a minor key ends with
a major tonic chord — the third of the chord is raised a half step to
create a major quality. Common in Baroque and Renaissance music, it
gives a feeling of finality and brightness at a cadence. The origin of
the French name is uncertain.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Picardy_third" target="_blank">1</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="core">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="timbre">timbre</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[tˈæmbəɹ]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-core">Core</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">The characteristic tone color or quality of a sound that distinguishes it from others at the same pitch.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>The quality of a sound that allows listeners to distinguish between
different sources even when pitch and loudness are the same. Timbre is
determined by a sound's harmonic content (the relative strength of its
overtones), attack, and decay. It is what makes a violin sound different
from a flute playing the same note, and is sometimes called "tone color."</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timbre" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#tone-colour">tone colour</a>, <a href="#acoustics">acoustics</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="tonal-tonality">tonal / tonality</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[toʊˈnælɪti]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">The organization of music around a central pitch (the tonic) using major or minor scales.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>The system of pitch organization in which a central note — the tonic —
functions as a point of rest and resolution, and all other pitches
relate to it in a hierarchy of tension and release. Tonality, using
major and minor scales and their associated harmonies, dominated Western
music from roughly 1600 to 1900. Music that avoids this system is
described as atonal or non-tonal.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tonality" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#atonal">atonal</a>, <a href="#modulation-in-music">modulation</a>, <a href="#key-change">key change</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="italian" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="tremolo">tremolo</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[tˈɹɛməloʊ]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Italian</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">A rapid fluctuation in volume, or rapid reiteration of a note.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>A rapid, repeated fluctuation in the volume (amplitude) of a note,
distinct from vibrato, which is a fluctuation in pitch. On string
instruments, tremolo is produced by rapidly repeating a note with the
bow; on piano, by rapid alternation between notes. In electronic music,
a tremolo effect is produced by a low-frequency oscillator modulating
amplitude. Note: the whammy bar on electric guitar is sometimes
incorrectly called a "tremolo arm" — it actually produces pitch variation
(vibrato).</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tremolo" target="_blank">1</a>, <a href="https://www.masterclass.com/articles/vibrato-voice" target="_blank">2</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#vibrato">vibrato</a>, <a href="#lfo">LFO</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="trill">trill</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[tɹɪl]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">Rapid alternation between a note and the note a step above it.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>An ornament consisting of rapid alternation between a written note and
the note a half or whole step above it. Trills are indicated in notation
by the symbol <strong>tr</strong> and were especially prevalent in Baroque and
Classical music. The speed and manner of beginning and ending a trill
vary by historical period and style.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trill_(music)" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#ornamentation">ornamentation</a>, <a href="#acciaccatura">acciaccatura</a>, <a href="#appoggiatura">appoggiatura</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="tuning">tuning</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[tjˈuːnɪŋ]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">The process of adjusting an instrument&#x27;s pitches to match a standard or system.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>The process of adjusting the pitch of an instrument so that its notes
correspond to a defined standard or system. Tuning may refer to adjusting
individual strings, pipes, or keys to the correct frequency, or to the
broader choice of tuning system (equal temperament, just intonation,
etc.) used as a reference.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musical_tuning" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#temperament">temperament</a>, <a href="#microtone">microtone</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="unison">unison</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[jˈuːnɪsən]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">Two or more voices or instruments performing the same pitch simultaneously.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>The simultaneous sounding of the same pitch by two or more performers,
or the same melody in multiple voices at the same pitch level (as
distinct from octaves). Unison playing creates a thicker, more powerful
sound on a single line and is used for emphasis, textural contrast, or
blend. In orchestral writing, unison passages are a common way to
reinforce a melody across sections.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unison" target="_blank">1</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="variation">variation</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[ˌvɛɹiˈeɪʃən]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">A modified restatement of a theme, changing some but not all of its features.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>A compositional technique in which a theme is repeated with alterations
to melody, harmony, rhythm, texture, timbre, or dynamics while
retaining enough of the original to remain recognizable. Theme and
variations is a common formal structure in Western classical music;
variation also occurs informally within improvised jazz.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variation_(music)" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#theme-and-variations">theme and variations</a>, <a href="#development">development</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="italian" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="verismo">verismo</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[vɛˈɹɪzmoʊ]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Italian</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">A late 19th-century Italian operatic style depicting realistic, everyday subjects.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>An Italian operatic movement of the late 19th and early 20th centuries
that rejected mythological and aristocratic subjects in favor of
realistic portrayals of ordinary people and contemporary life. Key
composers include Pietro Mascagni (<strong>Cavalleria rusticana</strong>) and Giacomo
Puccini. The style is characterized by intense dramatic emotion, lyrical
vocal writing, and vivid orchestration.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Verismo_(music)" target="_blank">1</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="italian" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="vibrato">vibrato</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[vɪˈbɹɑːtoʊ]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Italian</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">A rapid, slight fluctuation of pitch used to add warmth and expression to a note.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>A performance technique in which the pitch of a sustained note oscillates
rapidly and slightly above and below the central pitch, typically at a
rate of 5–7 cycles per second and within a range of less than a semitone.
Used in both vocal and instrumental music to add warmth, expression, and
resonance. Distinct from tremolo, which is a fluctuation in volume rather
than pitch. Different instruments employ different physical mechanisms:
finger movement on strings, breath variation on winds, and natural
laryngeal oscillation in singing.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vibrato" target="_blank">1</a>, <a href="https://www.masterclass.com/articles/vibrato-voice" target="_blank">2</a>, <a href="https://www.britannica.com/art/vibrato" target="_blank">3</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#tremolo">tremolo</a>, <a href="#timbre">timbre</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="expert">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="vocoder">vocoder</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[voʊkoʊdəɹ]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-expert">Expert</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">A device that imposes the spectral characteristics of one sound (usually voice) onto another.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>A signal processor that analyzes the frequency spectrum of one audio
source (the modulator, typically a voice) and applies that spectral
envelope to another source (the carrier, typically a synthesizer). The
result gives the carrier the impression of speaking or singing. Originally
developed for speech compression by Bell Labs in the 1930s, the vocoder
became an iconic electronic music effect in the 1970s and continues to
be widely used.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vocoder" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#synthesis">synthesis</a>, <a href="#effects">effects</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="voicing">voicing</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[vˈɔɪsɪŋ]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">The specific arrangement of notes within a chord, including register and spacing.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>The distribution of the notes of a chord among the available voices or
instruments, including decisions about register, spacing, and doubling.
Two chords may contain the same pitches but differ significantly in
character depending on how those pitches are arranged. Closely spaced
voicings (close position) produce a dense sound; widely spaced voicings
(open position) produce a more transparent texture. Voicing is a central
skill in arranging, piano comping, and choral writing.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voicing_(music)" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#chord">chord</a>, <a href="#inversion">inversion</a>, <a href="#texture">texture</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="technology" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="vst">VST</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[viː ɛs tiː]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Technology</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">Virtual Studio Technology — a standard for software audio plugins.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>A plugin format developed by Steinberg that allows software instruments
(VST instruments) and effects (VST effects) to be used within a DAW.
VST has become the most widely supported plugin format, with thousands
of commercial and free instruments and effects available.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virtual_Studio_Technology" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#daw">DAW</a>, <a href="#plug-in">plug-in</a>, <a href="#synthesis">synthesis</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="walking-bass">walking bass</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[wˈɔːkɪŋ beɪs]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">A bass line of steady quarter notes that outlines the chord changes.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>A style of bass accompaniment common in jazz, blues, and Baroque music,
consisting of continuous quarter notes that create a feeling of forward
motion. <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bassline">Walking bass lines</a>
use a mixture of chord tones, arpeggios, chromatic runs, and passing
tones to outline the chord progression, often with a melodic shape that
alternately rises and falls in pitch. The term originates from the
footstep-like regularity of the rhythm.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bassline" target="_blank">1</a>, <a href="https://jazznightschool.org/pages/walking-bass-lines-introduction-part-1" target="_blank">2</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#bass-line">bass line</a>, <a href="#basso-continuo">basso continuo</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="expert">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="wavetable-synthesis">wavetable synthesis</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[wˈeɪvteɪbəl sˈɪnθəsɪs]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-expert">Expert</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">A synthesis method that cycles through stored digital waveforms to produce sound.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>A digital synthesis technique in which a stored table of single-cycle
waveforms is read repeatedly to produce a tone. What distinguishes
wavetable synthesis from simple sampling is the ability to morph or
scan through multiple waveforms over time, creating evolving timbres.
Invented by Max Mathews in 1958 and developed for hardware synthesizers
by Wolfgang Palm (PPG) in the late 1970s, the technique became
ubiquitous in software synthesis through instruments such as Native
Instruments Massive and Xfer Serum.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wavetable_synthesis" target="_blank">1</a>, <a href="https://blog.native-instruments.com/what-is-wavetable-synthesis/" target="_blank">2</a>, <a href="https://splice.com/blog/what-is-wavetable-synthesis/" target="_blank">3</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#subtractive-synthesis">subtractive synthesis</a>, <a href="#fm-synthesis">FM synthesis</a>, <a href="#granular-synthesis">granular synthesis</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="wet-dry-signal">wet/dry signal</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[wɛt draɪ sɪɡnəl]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">Dry = unprocessed audio; wet = audio with effects applied.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>A dry signal is the original, unprocessed audio as captured or generated
before any effects are applied. A wet signal is that same audio after
passing through one or more effects processors — reverb, delay, chorus,
distortion, etc. In most effects units and plugins, a wet/dry (or
mix) knob blends the two, allowing the producer to dial in the amount
of effect without replacing the source sound entirely.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://www.differencebetween.net/technology/difference-between-wet-and-dry-signals-or-sounds/" target="_blank">1</a>, <a href="https://asmr.education/faq/music-mixing/dry-signal-vs-wet-signal" target="_blank">2</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#reverb">reverb</a>, <a href="#effects">effects</a>, <a href="#signal-processing-audio">signal processing</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="core">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="12-bar-blues">12-bar blues</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[twɛlv bɑːɹ bluːz]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-core">Core</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">A repeating 12-measure harmonic framework foundational to blues, jazz, and rock.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>A repeating harmonic and formal pattern of twelve bars that is the
foundational framework of blues music and has influenced jazz, rhythm
and blues, rock and roll, and country. The basic form uses three chords:
I (bars 1–4), IV (bars 5–6), I (bars 7–8), V (bar 9), IV (bar 10),
I (bars 11–12). Countless variations exist, particularly in jazz
(the "rhythm changes" is a contrasting alternative).</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twelve-bar_blues" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#blues-scale">blues scale</a>, <a href="#riff">riff</a>, <a href="#form">form</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="general" data-importance="enriching">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="12-note-techniques">12-note techniques</h3>
    <span class="term-pronunciation">[twɛlv noʊt tɛkˈniːk]</span>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">General</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-enriching">Enriching</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">A compositional method using a fixed ordering of all twelve chromatic pitches as the basis for a piece.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>A compositional method developed by Arnold Schoenberg in the early
1920s in which all twelve chromatic pitches are arranged into a fixed
ordered series (tone row or set). The row and its three transformations
— inversion (I), retrograde (R), and retrograde inversion (RI) — form
the exclusive pitch material of the piece. Adopted and developed by
Webern and Berg (the Second Viennese School) and later by Stravinsky,
Dallapiccola, and others.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Sources: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twelve-tone_technique" target="_blank">1</a></span>
      <span>See also: <a href="#atonal">atonal</a>, <a href="#retrograde">retrograde</a>, <a href="#inversion">inversion</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="rubric" data-importance="core">

  </div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="rubric" data-importance="core">

    <span class="imp-badge imp-core">Core</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">Combine or gather pre-existing material without change.</p>
  <div class="term-details">

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="rubric" data-importance="core">

    <span class="imp-badge imp-core">Core</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">Imitate with lack of detail.</p>
  <div class="term-details">

      <span>Source: DP Music Subject Guide</span>
      <span>Used in: <a href="rubrics.html#emc-c1,rt-approximate">EMC C1</a>, <a href="rubrics.html#pm-b,rt-approximate">PM B</a>, <a href="rubrics.html#pm-c,rt-approximate">PM C</a>, <a href="rubrics.html#cmm-c,rt-approximate">CMM C</a></span>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="rubric" data-importance="core">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">

    <span class="imp-badge imp-core">Core</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">Repeat or restate, largely without change.</p>
  <div class="term-details">

      <span>Source: DP Music Subject Guide</span>
      <span>Used in: <a href="rubrics.html#ewm-b,rt-reiterate">EWM B</a>, <a href="rubrics.html#ewm-d,rt-reiterate">EWM D</a></span>

</div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="rubric" data-importance="core">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>

  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>A Level 2 assessment term for research and written work. Description gives a detailed account but does not yet analyze causes or implications.</p></div>

      <span>Used in: <a href="rubrics.html#emc-b1,rt-describe">EMC B1</a>, <a href="rubrics.html#emc-b2,rt-describe">EMC B2</a>, <a href="rubrics.html#ewm-a,rt-describe">EWM A</a>, <a href="rubrics.html#ewm-c,rt-describe">EWM C</a>, <a href="rubrics.html#pm-a,rt-describe">PM A</a>, <a href="rubrics.html#cmm-b,rt-describe">CMM B</a></span>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="rubric" data-importance="core">

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="rubric" data-importance="core">

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="rubric" data-importance="core">

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="rubric" data-importance="core">

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="rubric" data-importance="core">

    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Rubric</span></div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="rubric" data-importance="core">

  <div class="term-header">

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="rubric" data-importance="core">

  <div class="term-details">

      <span>Used in: <a href="rubrics.html#ewm-a,rt-evaluate">EWM A</a>, <a href="rubrics.html#ewm-c,rt-evaluate">EWM C</a>, <a href="rubrics.html#cmm-b,rt-evaluate">CMM B</a></span>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="rubric" data-importance="core">

    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Source: DP Music Subject Guide</span>
      <span>Used in: <a href="rubrics.html#pm-c,rt-personalize">PM C</a>, <a href="rubrics.html#cmm-c,rt-personalize">CMM C</a></span>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="rubric" data-importance="core">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="rt-synthesize">Synthesize</h3>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Rubric</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-core">Core</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">Combine and blend existing elements, styles, or techniques to create new work.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>A Level 4 assessment term for practical work. Synthesizing goes beyond adaptation to produce something genuinely new from existing elements.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Source: DP Music Subject Guide</span>
      <span>Used in: <a href="rubrics.html#pm-b,rt-synthesize">PM B</a></span>

  </div>

<div class="term-entry" data-cats="rubric" data-importance="core">
  <span class="expand-hint">▸</span>
  <div class="term-header">
    <h3 class="term-title" id="rt-transform">Transform</h3>
    <div class="term-cats"><span class="term-cat">Rubric</span></div>
    <span class="imp-badge imp-core">Core</span>
  </div>
  <p class="term-short">Change and develop existing work to create new work.</p>
  <div class="term-details">
    <div class="term-long"><p>A Level 4 assessment term for practical work. Transforming fundamentally reimagines source material, creating work with a new identity and purpose.</p></div>
    <div class="term-meta-row">
      <span>Source: DP Music Subject Guide</span>
      <span>Used in: <a href="rubrics.html#ewm-b,rt-transform">EWM B</a>, <a href="rubrics.html#ewm-d,rt-transform">EWM D</a></span>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<p class="no-results" id="no-results" style="display:none;">No terms match the current filters.</p>
</div>

<table class="condensed-table" id="condensed-view">
  <thead>
    <tr>
      <th style="width:22%">Term</th>
      <th>Short definition</th>
      <th style="width:18%">Categories</th>
    </tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody id="condensed-body"></tbody>
</table>

```{=html}
<script>
(function(){
  var terms = Array.from(document.querySelectorAll('.term-entry'));
  var catAllCb = document.getElementById('cat-all');
  var catChecks = [];
  var catTrigger = document.getElementById('cat-trigger');
  var catPanel = document.getElementById('cat-panel');
  var logicOr = document.getElementById('logic-or');
  var logicAnd = document.getElementById('logic-and');
  var noResults = document.getElementById('no-results');
  var resultsCount = document.getElementById('results-count');
  var expandedView = document.getElementById('expanded-view');
  var condensedView = document.getElementById('condensed-view');
  var condensedBody = document.getElementById('condensed-body');
  var viewExpanded = document.getElementById('view-expanded');
  var viewCondensed = document.getElementById('view-condensed');
  var viewFull = document.getElementById('view-full');
  var sortBtns = Array.from(document.querySelectorAll('.sort-btn'));

  (function buildCatList() {
    var catCounts = {};
    terms.forEach(function(t) {
      t.dataset.cats.split(' ').forEach(function(c) { catCounts[c] = (catCounts[c]||0)+1; });
    });
    var cats = Object.keys(catCounts).sort();
    var CAT_LABELS = {
      'roman-numeral':'Roman Numerals','italian':'Italian','harmony':'Harmony',
      'technology':'Technology','non-western':'Non-Western','vocal':'Vocal',
      'form':'Form','homograph':'Homograph','general':'General'
    };
    function toLabel(s){ return CAT_LABELS[s]||s.replace(/-/g,' ').replace(/^./,function(c){return c.toUpperCase();}); }
    var list = document.getElementById('cat-list');
    cats.forEach(function(cat){
      var label = document.createElement('label');
      label.innerHTML = '<input type="checkbox" class="cat-check" value="'+cat+'"> '
        +toLabel(cat)+' <span style="color:#aaa;font-size:0.78em;">('+catCounts[cat]+')</span>';
      list.appendChild(label);
    });
    catChecks = Array.from(document.querySelectorAll('.cat-check'));
    catChecks.forEach(function(c){
      c.addEventListener('change', function(){
        if(c.checked) catAllCb.checked=false;
        if(catChecks.every(function(x){return !x.checked;})) catAllCb.checked=true;
        applyFilters();
      });
    });
  })();

  var logic = 'or';
  var currentView = 'expanded';
  var sortStack = [];
  var impActive = {core:true,enriching:true,expert:true};
  var impOrder  = {core:1,enriching:2,expert:3};

  document.querySelectorAll('.imp-btn').forEach(function(btn){
    btn.addEventListener('click',function(){
      var level=btn.dataset.level;
      impActive[level]=!impActive[level];
      btn.classList.toggle('active',impActive[level]);
      applyFilters();
    });
  });

  function getTermValue(term,key){
    if(key==='alpha') return term.querySelector('.term-title').textContent.toLowerCase();
    if(key==='category') return term.dataset.cats.split(' ')[0];
    if(key==='importance') return String(impOrder[term.dataset.importance]||9);
    return '';
  }
  function sortedTerms(arr){
    if(!sortStack.length) return arr;
    return arr.slice().sort(function(a,b){
      for(var i=0;i<sortStack.length;i++){
        var s=sortStack[i]; var va=getTermValue(a,s.key); var vb=getTermValue(b,s.key);
        if(va<vb) return s.dir==='asc'?-1:1; if(va>vb) return s.dir==='asc'?1:-1;
      }
      return 0;
    });
  }
  function updateSortButtons(){
    sortBtns.forEach(function(btn){
      var key=btn.dataset.key; var idx=sortStack.findIndex(function(s){return s.key===key;});
      var dirSpan=btn.querySelector('.sort-dir'); var badge=btn.querySelector('.sort-badge');
      if(badge) btn.removeChild(badge);
      if(idx===-1){ btn.classList.remove('active'); dirSpan.textContent='↑'; dirSpan.style.color='#ddd'; }
      else{
        btn.classList.add('active'); dirSpan.textContent=sortStack[idx].dir==='asc'?'↑':'↓'; dirSpan.style.color='#2c2416';
        if(sortStack.length>1){ var b=document.createElement('span'); b.className='sort-badge'; b.textContent=idx+1; btn.insertBefore(b,btn.firstChild); }
      }
    });
  }
  sortBtns.forEach(function(btn){
    btn.addEventListener('click',function(){
      var key=btn.dataset.key; var idx=sortStack.findIndex(function(s){return s.key===key;});
      var def='asc';
      if(idx===-1){ sortStack.unshift({key:key,dir:def}); if(sortStack.length>4) sortStack.pop(); }
      else if(sortStack[idx].dir===def){ sortStack[idx].dir='desc'; var item=sortStack.splice(idx,1)[0]; sortStack.unshift(item); }
      else{ sortStack.splice(idx,1); }
      updateSortButtons(); applyFilters();
    });
  });

  catTrigger.addEventListener('click',function(e){ e.stopPropagation(); catPanel.classList.toggle('open'); });
  document.addEventListener('click',function(){ catPanel.classList.remove('open'); });
  catPanel.addEventListener('click',function(e){ e.stopPropagation(); });
  catAllCb.addEventListener('change',function(){ if(catAllCb.checked) catChecks.forEach(function(c){c.checked=false;}); applyFilters(); });
  [logicOr,logicAnd].forEach(function(btn){
    btn.addEventListener('click',function(){
      logic=btn.dataset.logic; logicOr.classList.toggle('active',logic==='or'); logicAnd.classList.toggle('active',logic==='and'); applyFilters();
    });
  });

  function setView(v){
    currentView=v;
    viewExpanded.classList.toggle('active',v==='expanded');
    viewCondensed.classList.toggle('active',v==='condensed');
    viewFull.classList.toggle('active',v==='compact');
    expandedView.style.display=(v==='condensed')?'none':'';
    condensedView.style.display=(v==='condensed')?'table':'none';
    condensedView.classList.toggle('active',v==='condensed');
    if(v==='compact'){ terms.forEach(function(t){ var d=t.querySelector('.term-details'); var h=t.querySelector('.expand-hint'); if(d) d.classList.add('open'); if(h) h.textContent='▾'; }); }
    else if(v==='expanded'){ terms.forEach(function(t){ var d=t.querySelector('.term-details'); var h=t.querySelector('.expand-hint'); if(d) d.classList.remove('open'); if(h) h.textContent='▸'; }); }
    applyFilters();
  }
  viewFull.addEventListener('click',function(){ setView('compact'); });
  viewExpanded.addEventListener('click',function(){ setView('expanded'); });
  viewCondensed.addEventListener('click',function(){ setView('condensed'); });

  terms.forEach(function(term){
    term.addEventListener('click',function(e){
      if(currentView==='compact') return;
      if(e.target.closest('select,a,input')) return;
      var details=term.querySelector('.term-details'); var hint=term.querySelector('.expand-hint');
      var open=details.classList.toggle('open'); if(hint) hint.textContent=open?'▾':'▸';
    });
  });

  function updateTriggerLabel(){
    var checked=catChecks.filter(function(c){return c.checked;}).map(function(c){return c.parentElement.textContent.trim();});
    catTrigger.textContent=checked.length===0?'All categories ▾':checked.length===1?checked[0]+' ▾':checked.length+' categories ▾';
  }
  function termVisible(term){
    var termCats=term.dataset.cats.split(' ');
    var selected=catChecks.filter(function(c){return c.checked;}).map(function(c){return c.value;});
    var catMatch;
    if(selected.length===0||catAllCb.checked){ catMatch=true; }
    else if(logic==='or'){ catMatch=selected.some(function(s){return termCats.indexOf(s)>-1;}); }
    else{ catMatch=selected.every(function(s){return termCats.indexOf(s)>-1;}); }
    var impLevel=term.dataset.importance||'enriching';
    return catMatch && impActive[impLevel]!==false;
  }
  function buildCondensed(visibleTerms){
    condensedBody.innerHTML='';
    visibleTerms.forEach(function(term){
      var titleEl=term.querySelector('.term-title'); var shortEl=term.querySelector('.term-short');
      if(!titleEl||!shortEl) return;
      var title=titleEl.textContent; var shortDef=shortEl.textContent;
      var cats=Array.from(term.querySelectorAll('.term-cat')).map(function(c){return c.textContent;}).join(', ');
      var longEl=term.querySelector('.term-long'); var long=longEl?longEl.innerHTML:'';
      var metaEl=term.querySelector('.term-meta-row'); var meta=metaEl?metaEl.outerHTML:'';
      var tr=document.createElement('tr');
      tr.innerHTML='<td class="ct-term">'+title+'</td><td class="ct-def">'+shortDef+'</td><td style="font-size:0.72rem;color:#888;white-space:nowrap;">'+cats+'</td>';
      var expTr=document.createElement('tr'); expTr.className='condensed-expanded';
      expTr.innerHTML='<td colspan="3"><p style="font-size:0.86rem;color:#555;margin:0 0 0.5rem;">'+long+'</p>'+meta+'</td>';
      tr.addEventListener('click',function(){ var wasOpen=expTr.classList.contains('open'); document.querySelectorAll('.condensed-expanded').forEach(function(r){r.classList.remove('open');}); if(!wasOpen) expTr.classList.add('open'); });
      condensedBody.appendChild(tr); condensedBody.appendChild(expTr);
    });
  }
  function applyFilters(){
    updateTriggerLabel();
    var visible=sortedTerms(terms.filter(function(t){return termVisible(t);}));
    var hiddenSet=terms.filter(function(t){return !termVisible(t);});
    var container=document.getElementById('expanded-view');
    visible.forEach(function(t){container.appendChild(t);}); hiddenSet.forEach(function(t){t.style.display='none';}); visible.forEach(function(t){t.style.display='';});
    noResults.style.display=visible.length===0?'':'none';
    resultsCount.textContent=visible.length===terms.length?terms.length+' terms':visible.length+' of '+terms.length+' terms';
    if(currentView==='condensed') buildCondensed(visible);
  }
  // ── State persistence: save/restore filter+sort+view across navigation ──────
  var GLKEY='gl_state';
  function saveState(){try{var cats=catChecks.filter(function(c){return c.checked;}).map(function(c){return c.value;});sessionStorage.setItem(GLKEY,JSON.stringify({cats:cats,allCats:catAllCb.checked,logic:logic,imp:impActive,sort:sortStack,view:currentView,sy:window.scrollY}));}catch(e){}}
  [viewFull,viewExpanded,viewCondensed].forEach(function(b){b.addEventListener('click',function(){setTimeout(saveState,0);});});
  sortBtns.forEach(function(b){b.addEventListener('click',function(){setTimeout(saveState,0);});});
  [logicOr,logicAnd].forEach(function(b){b.addEventListener('click',function(){setTimeout(saveState,0);});});
  document.querySelectorAll('.imp-btn').forEach(function(b){b.addEventListener('click',function(){setTimeout(saveState,0);});});
  catAllCb.addEventListener('change',function(){setTimeout(saveState,0);});
  catChecks.forEach(function(c){c.addEventListener('change',function(){setTimeout(saveState,0);});});
  window.addEventListener('pagehide',saveState);
  (function(){
    var raw; try{raw=sessionStorage.getItem(GLKEY);}catch(e){}
    if(!raw){sortStack=[{key:'alpha',dir:'asc'}];updateSortButtons();setView('compact');return;}
    var s; try{s=JSON.parse(raw);}catch(e){sortStack=[{key:'alpha',dir:'asc'}];updateSortButtons();setView('compact');return;}
    if(!s.allCats&&s.cats){catAllCb.checked=false;catChecks.forEach(function(c){c.checked=s.cats.indexOf(c.value)>-1;});}
    if(s.logic){logic=s.logic;logicOr.classList.toggle('active',logic==='or');logicAnd.classList.toggle('active',logic==='and');}
    if(s.imp){impActive=s.imp;document.querySelectorAll('.imp-btn').forEach(function(b){b.classList.toggle('active',impActive[b.dataset.level]!==false);});}
    sortStack=s.sort||[{key:'alpha',dir:'asc'}];updateSortButtons();
    setView(s.view||'compact');
    if(s.sy)setTimeout(function(){window.scrollTo(0,s.sy);},100);
  })();
  (function(){var h=window.location.hash;if(!h)return;if(h.startsWith('#glterm=')){var id=h.slice(8);var el=document.getElementById(id);if(el){var entry=el.closest('.term-entry')||el;history.replaceState(null,'',window.location.pathname+window.location.search);setTimeout(function(){entry.scrollIntoView({behavior:'smooth',block:'center'});entry.classList.add('glterm-highlight');},120);}}else{try{var t=document.querySelector(h);if(t)setTimeout(function(){t.scrollIntoView({behavior:'smooth',block:'start'});},80);}catch(e){}}})();
})();
</script>
```
